case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 23.02.2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos.3992 & 2974 of 1999.)
full_judgment:
M.M. Ruhul Amin J: These two petitions for leave to appeal are directed against the common judgment and order dated 23.02.2005 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision Nos.3992 & 2974 of 1999 discharging both the Rules.

2. Short facts are that the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.66 of 1991 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Additional Court, Dhaka for declaration that the judgment and decree dated 05.06.1980 passed in Title Suit No.346 of 1977 by the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge). Dhaka is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff stating, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Priaya Nath Basak, Nagendra Nath Basak, Bhupendra Nath Basak and Digendra Nath Basak who were owners of the suit land to the extent of 4 annas share each and their names were correctly recorded in the S.A. Khatian and that during 1965 war between India and Pakistan the aforesaid. S.A. recorded owners left the country for India and the suit land was declared and treated as enemy property (now vested property) The suit land was leased out to one Abdul Baten in E.P. Case No.210 of 1967 and subsequently lease was granted to Rahmat-E-Alam Islam Mission who also paid lease money up 1385 B.S. The further allegation is that the defendant obtained an exparte decree in Title Suit No.346 of 1977 on 06.05.1980 declaring that the suit land is not vested and non-resident property and it was their purchased land from Rathindra Nath Basak who was the adopted son of Debendra Nath Basak by registered kabala dated 21.07.1977. The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka was impleaded as a party in the said suit land but the Assistant Custodian of the vested and non-resident property was not impleaded in the suit as a party in Title Suit No.346 of 1977 and thus exparte decree dated 05.06.1980 is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Debendra Nath Basak, Lal Mohan Basak and Promotha Nath Basak and by an amicable partition, the suit land fell in the saham of Debendra Nath Basak, one of the sons of Modon Mohan Basak who got 4 annas share in the suit land. Debendra Nath Basak died issueless leaving behind only a widow who adopted a son named Rathindra Nath Basak and the suit land was recorded in the name of Rathindra Nath Basak on mutation in the S.A. Khatian and the defendants purchased the suit land from Rathindra Nath Basak by two separate registered kabalas on 21.07.1977 and got their names mutated in the Khatian. The defendant was compelled to file Title Suit No.346 of 1977 against the present plaintiff and other. The summons was duly served upon the plaintiff and others but none appeared to contest the suit and the suit was ultimately decreed exparte on 05.06.1980. The defendants then filed an application for correction of the S.A. record before the Circle Officer (Revenue) on the basis of the decree passed in Title Suit No.346 of 1977 and when the matter was placed before the Circle Officer he refused the proposal for correction on the ground that  the suit land was declared vested and non-vested property. It was further alleged that the suit land was leased out to one Monir Hossein and others and subsequently to defendant No.12 who was put in possession in respect of 13.70 acres of land and has been possessing the same. The further allegation is that the defendant Nos.1-11 of Title Suit N6.346 of 1977 obtained an exparte decree though they were not owners of the suit land. It was further alleged that adoption Rathindra Nath Basak was illegal and invalid.

4. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff. The defendants then preferred Title Suit No.357 of 1992. The appellate court allowed the appeal and dismissed the plaintiffs suit. Being aggrieved thereby the plaintiff being the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) in charge of the vested and non-resident property Dhaka moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rules. The defendant No.12, Secretary, Rahmat-E-Alam Islam Mission and Etimkhana as petitioner has obtained another Rule being Civil Revision No.2974 of 1999. Since both the Rules arising out of self-same judgment of the appellate court, were heard together and disposed of by the impugned judgment the High Court Division upon hearing the parties discharging the Rules as noticed earlier.

5. We have heard Mr. Fazlul Haque, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in both the cases and Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for respondent Nos.1-10 in both the cases and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers.

<u>6. The High Court Division held that there is nothing on record to indicate that any vested property case was started in respect of the suit land but from the evidence on record it was found that the Title Suit No.346 of 1977 was decreed exparte on 05.06.1980. The High Court Division held that this will be sometimes after 1980 as the exparte decree was passed on 05.06.1980 and the law on enemy property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance 1 of 1969 with effect from 23.03.1974 and no further vested property case could be started thereafter. Accordingly, the High Court Division held that the plaintiff having failed to prove that the S.A. recorded tenants left for India in 1965 and the suit land became enemy property, he has no locus standi to challenge the decree passed in Title Suit No.346 of 1977. The High Court Division further observed that P.W.1 admitted that the summons of Title Suit No.346 of 1977 was served upon the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka. There is no evidence of any fraud practiced upon the party or, upon the court in obtaining the decree in Title Suit No.346 of 1977. Non-inclusion of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) in charge of vested property is not a fraudulent act to turn down the earlier decree on the ground of fraud are rightly held by the lower appellate court that non-joinder of a party may not defeat the suit is all cases. The High Court Division further held, "I have examined the documentary evidence and the oral evidence but I could not find out any materials indicating that any fraud was practiced upon the party or the court in obtaining the decree in Title Suit No.346 of 1977. The learned Advocate for the petitioners could not point out any evidence indicating fraud committed by the plaintiffs of the earlier suit in obtaining the earlier exparte decree, I do not therefore, find any error of law committed by the lower appellate court in dismissing the plaintiffs suit. The trial court made a totally   wrong approach to the pleading of the parties and the evidence on record." The High Court Division further held that non-inclusion of a party cannot be construed as a fraud.</u>

7. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka who was in charge of vested and non-resident property was not a party in Title Suit No.346 of 1977 and as such the decree is not binding on him. Therefore, the decree is liable to be set aside. In this connection it may be stated that since the petitioner was not party to the decree, the same is not automatically binding on him. Avoid decree need to be avoided by a decree of a competent court but avoidable decree need be avoided by a decree of the court of competent jurisdiction. Therefore no suit is maintainable at the instance of such a party for declaration that the decree passed in such a suit is not binding on him.

8. In the case of Munsur Ali Mallik Vs. Md. Nurul Haque Mallik and others reported in BCR 1986(AD)56 the plaintiff challenged the decree obtained in Title Suit No.69 of 1961 by one Lakshman Chandra Dhupi, predecessor of the defendant. In the suit, the plaintiff was not a party. In the second appeal, the High Court Division considered the submission exhaustively and it was noticed that in the suit of Lakshman Chandra Dhupi, the plaintiff, was not a party. Hence the suit for declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No. 69 of 1961 at the instance of Lakshman Chandra Dhupi could not be entertained. In this view of the matter, the appeal was dismissed.

9. In the facts and circumstances of the case and in view of the discussions made above, we are of the view that the High Court Division upon correct assessment of the materials on record arrived at a correct decision. There is no cogent reason to interfere with the impugned judgment.

10. Both the civil petitions accordingly are dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
S.K. Sinha J: In this appeal leave was granted on two points. The first point is that if two sale deeds are executed by the same vendor in respect of the same lands in favour of two different persons on two different dates and if the deed which was executed subsequently was registered earlier than the other deed whether the deed which was registered earlier would take effect from the date of its registration or from the date of its execution. The Second point is whether a decree declaring a registered deed void can be passed, which was executed and registered through Court in execution of a decree passed by a competent Court without setting aside the decree.

2. Respondent No.1 (the plaintiff) instituted the suit in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Narayangonj for declaration that the deed dated 14th November, 1992 executed and registered through Court in pursuance of the decree passed in Title Suit No.14 of 1986 is fraudulent, illegal, inoperative and void for confirmation of possession and permanent injunction, alleging inter alia that the lands covered by the impugned deed belonged to Abdul Barek and Abdul Mannan (vendors) who proposed to sell the same and the plaintiff agreed to purchase the same at Tk. 5,89,000/. Pursuant thereto, the parties entered into an agreement for sale on 27th March, 1984 and the plaintiff having paid an advance sum of Tk. 1,00,000/- the vendors, defendant Nos. 2 and 3, handed over possession of the suit lands on that day and since then he has been continuing in possession. The vendors thereupon executed and registered a sale deed in favour of the plaintiff on receipt of the balance consideration amount on 21st October, 1992. The appellant (the defendant), it is alleged, in collusion with others claimed title and interest in the suit lands which clouded the plaintiffs title. Subsequently, the plaintiff came to know that the defendant entered into a transaction with his vendors on 24th April, 1984 and obtained a decree in Title Suit No.14 of 1986 in respect of the suit lands which is fraudulent and not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement claiming, inter alia, that the vendors sold .49 acres of land out of the suit Nos.184, 404 and the other owners Mari Bibi and Banu Bibi executed an agreement for sale on 24th April, 1984 in respect of some lands out of same plot's on receipt of advance money and handed over possession of the suit lands on the same day. When the vendors refused to execute a sale deed the defendant instituted Title Suit No.14 of 1986 for specific performance of contract and obtained a decree On 24th May, 1989. Pursuant thereto, he got a sale deed duly executed and registered through Court and also got formal possession of the suit lands through Court. His further case is that the plaintiffs deed of agreement for sale dated 27th March, 1984 is ante-dated and collusive one, created for the purpose of grabbing the suit lands.

4. The trial Court on assessment of the evidence on record decreed the suit. On appeal by the defendant from the said judgment and decree, a Division Bench of the High Court Division affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

5. The learned Judges of the High Court Division while affirming those of the trial Court observed that the trial Court rightly believed the execution of the deed of agreement for sale dated 27th March, 1984 by the vendors, in favour of the plaintiff and delivery of possession on that date, and also rightly believed the deed of the plaintiff dated 21st October, 1992 as genuine one. The learned Judges further held that section 47 of the Registration Act, 1908 would not be attracted in this case, inasmuch as, in order to attract section 47, the documents must be at par and on the same footing and that as such, the trial Court correctly found that the deed of the defendant is false and collusive one and it was not acted upon.

6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing for the defendant argued that the learned Judges of the High Court Division committed a fundamental error in taking the plaintiffs deed of agreement for sale as the basis for passing a decree in contravention to section 47 of the Registration Act, wherein it is provided that a deed of sale takes effect from the date of its execution and since the defendant's deed was executed prior in point of time it would take effect earlier than that of the plaintiff but the learned Judges on a misconception of law failed to consider that aspect of the matter.

7. There is no dispute that the defendant had entered into an agreement for sale of the suit lands with the vendors on 24th April, 1984 and as the vendors did not execute the sale deed as per his demand, he instituted Title Suit No.14 of 1986 against the plaintiffs vendors and got a decree and in execution of the said decree, the defendant got the sale deed executed and registered through Court and also got the possession of the Suit lands. Admittedly, the defendant's deed was executed on 13th October, 1992 and registered on 14th November, 1992, where as, the plaintiffs deed was executed and registered on 21st October, 1992. Now the crux of the point is which deed will prevail. To resolve the said issue one aspect is required to be kept in mind is that after filing Title Suit No.14 of 1986, the vendors on receipt of the summons entered appearance and filed a written statement on 22nd July, 1986, ext-Gha, wherein the plaintiffs vendors did not say that they entered into an agreement for sale of the suit lands with the plaintiff on 27th March, 1984, rather stated that they entered into an agreement for sale on 10th November, 1985 with one Mokhlesur Rahman in respect of .70 acres out of the suit plots. They ultimately did not contest the suit.

8. Mr. Mahmudul Islam learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff contends that this written statement cannot be used in this suit since the averments made therein have not been proved in Court in accordance with law and secondly, those averments were made in a different suit in which the plaintiff was not a party and he was not afforded an opportunity to controvert those statements. This submission merits no consideration in view of the fact that this written statement has been admitted into evidence as ext- Ga and if the plaintiff disputes the averments made therein, he could have examined his vendors for ascertaining the truth or falsehood of the statements made therein. More so, the said written statement was filed by none other than the plaintiffs predecessors in respect of the suit lands before he had acquired any right or interest therein.

9. The plaintiffs vendors did not say that they entered into an agreement for sale of the suit lands with the plaintiff and delivered possession to him rather stated that they entered into such transaction with a third party. These being verified statements of the plaintiffs vendors, the plaintiff having claimed title through them, he stepped into the shoes of his vendors and therefore, he can not ignore those statements. Whatever rights he has acquired in respect of the suit lands are subject to what right his vendors had or liability incurred by them at the time of execution of the deed of agreement. He could not acquire better right or interest in the suit lands than his vendors. Therefore, we are of the view that there is no legal bar in taking consideration of the statements made in ext-Gha.

<u>10. An admission of a person is admissible in evidence as against him, though it can he explained away by the maker thereof or the person against whom it is sought lo be proved. According to me, the same principle applies to an admission in a signed pleading, or in affidavit, or in any swam deposition given by a party in a prior litigation, though it is capable of rebuttal. The assertion of a right, whether in a pleadings or other statements, is relevant under section 13 of the Evidence Act and is, therefore, legally admissible in evidence; Phipson on Evidence, Ninth Edition, at page 455 stated that "pleadings are admissible, in subsequent proceedings, to prove their own existence, the institution of the suit, and the facts in issue between the parties. But being regarded in other respects rather as the suggestions of counsel than the declarations of the parties, they are not receivable to prove the truth of the facts stated, even as admissions, unless verified by oath, or signed or otherwise specifically adopted by those against whom they are tendered". In Satyadeo Prasad V. Smt. Chanderjoti, AIR 1966 Pat 110, it was argued that an admission in a signed pleading filed in an earlier suit by the predecessor of the defendant could be used against his successor, inasmuch as, an admission contained in a plaint or written statement or an affidavit or any sworn deposition given by a party in a prior litigation will be regarded as an admission in a subsequent action, though it is capable, of rebuttal. Similar views have been taken in S.T. Chendikamba V. K.I. Biswanathamayya,  AIR 1939 Mad 446. It was pointed out that what a party himself admits to be true may reasonably be presumed to he so, but the party making the admission may give evidence to rebut this presumption and unless and until that is satisfactorily done the fact admitted must be taken to be established.</u>

11. While discarding the defendant's deed, the learned Judges of the High Court Division noticed the case of Rafiqul Islam (Md.) Vs. Mir Abul Ali, 44 DLR(AD)176 but failed to appreciate the statement of law argued therein. It was observed by Mustafa Kamal, J. that "when the same vendor executes and registers two sale deeds in respect of the same suit land in favour of two different purchasers on two different dates, section 47 of the Registration Act settles which one will prevail over the other. The sale deed which was executed later but registered earlier in point of time and the criterion in such cases for the purpose of determining when the sale lakes effect is not the date of registration but the date of execution of the sale deed itself'. The facts of the case are that the plaintiff purchased the suit land at Tk.3,000/- in 1974, whereas, the defendant purchased the Suit land at Tk.8,000/- in 1972. 130th the Courts below dismissed the suit but the High Court Division decreed the suit on the reasoning’s that the plaintiffs deed will prevail over the defendant's deed since the plaintiffs deed was registered earlier than that of the defendant. The Appellate Division reversed the judgment of the High Court Division and restored those of the Courts below. In view of such facts, Mustafa Kamal then observed "Section 47 of the Registration Act is attracted only when the two competing documents are otherwise at par and stand on the same footing". The High Court Division presumed the above observations are the ratio decidendi of the case in failing to notice that the above statements made in passing are in the nature of obiter dicta.

12. One fact the learned Judges failed to notice in thin regard is that the positive case of the defendant is that the plaintiffs deed of agreement for sale is a forged, collusive and ante dated one created with prior knowledge of the deed of agreement for sale executed by his vendors with the defendant. Exhibit-Ga, is an order of the High Court Division summarily rejecting provisional application being Civil Order No.1548 of 1993 moved by the plaintiff against an order rejecting his prayer for staying all further proceedings in Title Execution Case No.40 of 1989. This order proved that the plaintiff had no knowledge about the decree and that the claim that the defendant collusively obtained the deed proved negative. Both the deeds were executed within a space of 15 days and the difference of price in the two deeds is 41,000/- (Tk. 4,98,000/-Tk. 4,57.000/-) only. The High Court Division failed to consider that as the vendors were allured him to give higher price by the plaintiff, he executed the sale deed in his favour and with a view to justify the transaction, created an unregistered agreement giving a back date of its execution otherwise there was no reason to execute the sale deed after 8 years 7 months of the date of execution of the agreement on 27th March, 1984.

13. The High Court Division, in the premises, erred in law in holding that section 47 of the Registration Act is not applicable since the deeds were not at par. Section 47 of the Registration Act provides that a document shall operate from the time it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made and not from the time of its registration. There is no doubt that a document which requires registration so long it is not registered is not valid yet. Once it is registered it takes effect from the date of its execution. The object of this section 47 is to decide which of two or more registered instruments in respect of the same property is to have effect. A sale which is not complete until the registration of the document is complete, cannot be said to have been completed earlier because by virtue of section, 47 of the Registration. Act the instrument by which it is effected, after it has been registered, commences to operate from the date of its execution.

14. Mr. Mahmudul Islam having realised that the High Court Division misconstrued section 47 of the Registration Act, did not make any submission repelling the contention of Mr. Bhuiyan and endeavored to make out a case that in view of illustrations (g) and (h) of section 3 of the Specific Relief Act, the defendant having purchased the suit lands with notice of the plaintiffs possession, the defendant is trustee for the plaintiff and thus, the High Court Division is justified in maintaining the trial Court's decree. Learned Counsel further contended that the decree passed by the trial Court without setting aside the decree passed in Title Suit No.14 of 1986 is also in accordance with law. Learned counsel based his submission on the premises that both the High Court Division and the trial Court concurrently found that the plaintiff got possession in the suit lands from the date of execution of the deed of agreement on 27th March, 1984, and disbelieved the defendant's claim of getting possession firstly on 24th April 1984, and subsequently through Court in execution of the decree. According to Mr. Islam this finding of fact being based on the evidence on record should not be disturbed which is an established norm being followed by this Court. In this connection the learned Counsel has referred the case of Ramappa V. Bojjappa, AIR 1963 SC 1633.

15. We do not dispute the statements of law argued in the above case but we are afraid how the statements of law argued in the above case are applicable in this case? In that case the point was whether the High Court in exercise of powers under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure in a second appeal could disturb the findings of facts arrived at by the courts below. It was argued that if the High Court has contravened either willingly or in a casual manner the limits prescribed by section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure by interfering with the concurrent findings of fact, it is the duty of the Supreme Court to interfere. The Supreme Court then observed "It has been always recognised that sufficiency or adequacy of evidence to support a finding of fact is a matter for decision of the Court of facts and cannot be agitated in a second appeal".

16. We are not unmindful that this Court is loath to interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the High Court Division, but where the High Court Division failed to interfere when such interference was called for, or where on the evidence on the record no Court could, as a matter of legitimate inference, arrive at the conclusion that the finding is perverse or supported by no evidence but the High Court Division failed to exercise its jurisdiction against such perverse finding, or where the High Court Division was under a misapprehension as to the finding on a material fact, or where the approach of the High Court Division is basically wrong, or important and crucial evidence has been overlooked or wrongly appreciated or misread in arriving at the finding leading to injustice, or involves an error of law or relied on inadmissible evidence, or where the finding of fact arrived at without taking into Consideration the relevant oral and documentary evidence, or where conelusions arrived at by the High Court Division by misconstruing a provision of law, or where the High Court Division being the final Court of fact disregarded the principles concerning the approach to evidence or it committed grave error in appreciating the evidence, or where the finding of fact though is concurrent, there are any special reasons such as a manifest error of law in arriving at the finding, or where there is failure of justice due to non consideration of a material piece of evidence or the decision is manifestly unjust, or where the finding is perverse, it being such as no reasonable person could have arrived at even if the evidence was taken at its face value or where the finding is based and built on inadmissible evidence, which evidence, if excluded from vision, Would negate the case, this Division will examine the evidence on the point and in fit cases it will interfere with findings of fact.

17. Mr. Bhuiyan by taking to the relevant evidence of the Witnesses argues that the findings of possession arrived at by the trial Court and affirmed by the High Court Division are not only perverse but also based upon superficial consideration of the material evidence on record and thus, according to him, it is a fit case to interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the Courts below by the Division for ends of justice. On perusal of the judgments of the trial Court and the High Court Division it can not be said that the submission of Mr. Bhuiyan has no substance at all, inasmuch as, we have noticed inconsistencies in both the judgments on the point of findings of possession.

18. Each party has examined 4 witnesses in support of their respective possession. The learned Subordinate Judge though considered the evidence of PWs.1-4 but A did not base his decision relying upon P.W.1 and believed the plaintiffs possession relying upon the evidence of P.Ws.2- 4 as will be evident from his findings that "on perusal of the evidence of P W.2 to P.W.4 it is crystal the plaintiff had gone into possession of the suit land on 27.3.84 in execution of the bainapatra on the said date and got the due execution and registration of the kabala in his favour on 21.10.92 being marked as Ext.5. The genuineness, trustworthiness, credibility, authenticity and veracity of the bainapatra Ext.6 and the kabala Ext.5 thus get established without any shadow of doubt".

19. The High Court Division, on the other hand, on assessment of the evidence of both sides affirmed the findings of trial Court observing that: "The trial Court has considered the assertion in the agreement of the defendants dated 24.4.84 about the delivery of possession on that date and rightly observed that if the defendants were in possession on 24.4.84 there was no reason to get the delivery of possession through Court. Defendants own witnesses namely P.W.8 and 6 admitted that the defendants are not in possession of the suit land rather the suit land has been in possession of the plaintiff through P.W.2 Taizuddin their borgader. This finding of facts of the trial Court is based on proper appreciation of evidence which calls for no interference by this Court."

20. It would be evident from Ext-6, the plaintiffs unregistered deed of agreement for sale that Md. Taizuddin (P.W. 2) and one Md. Akkas Ali had been cited as witnesses. Hanif (P.W. 1), the attorney of the plaintiff is not a witness of this agreement and naturally he was not present at the time of transaction. Therefore, no reliance can be given as to his statement that the vendors on executing the agreement for sale handed over possession to the plaintiff on the same day and naturally the trial Court ignored his evidence. The plaintiff was present at the time of execution but his non-appearance and that of Md. Akkas Ali, to support the possession negatived the plaintiffs claim that he got possession on 27th March, 1984. Mr. Mahmudul Islam contends that in view of the proviso to Order III rule I of the code of Civil Procedure, there is no legal bar on the part of P.W.1 to depose on behalf of the plaintiff, inasmuch as, the clear intendment of this provision is that an appearance or act done by the party himself or by his recognised agent or by his lawyer, but the Court has jurisdiction to direct a party to appear in person and on his failure to do so, to dismiss the suit or proceed ex-parte. As the defendant, according to him, did not pray for appearance of the plaintiff for cross-examination, the defendant should not take any exception for his non-appearance.

21. We do not dispute to the proposition that a person duly authorised by a power of attorney by his principal can depose as a witness on behalf of his principal in a civil proceeding, but the question is the evidentiary value of a particular witness. Normally, an agent deposes on behalf of his principal in cases where the principal is incapable of giving evidence or is beyond the limits of the country or is sick and infirm, or his attendance can not be procured without an amount of delay which, under the circumstances of the case, would be unreasonable. None of these circumstances is present in this case and the plaintiff has totally failed to make out such a case. He simply stated in the power of attorney, ext-X, that he being a businessman remained busy with his business affairs, it was not possible on his part to prosecute the suit and accordingly appointed Md. Hanif for conducting the suit. These are not legal grounds for non-appearance of a vital witness. If he was at all busy, he could have been examined on commission.

22. The question is not the competency of P.W.1 to depose of behalf of the plaintiff. The question is reliability of a particular witness to prove a fact in issue. The first duty of a Court being to ascertain facts about which the parties are at issue. Section 5 of the Evidence Act may be described as the corner stone of the structure of Part-I of the Evidence Act which specifies the facts that may be given in evidence. Since a fact in issue is the necessary ingredient of the litigated right or liability, it may be given in evidence as a matter of course. It is a fundamental rule that unless there is some presumption as to existence of a fact, its existence must be proved to the satisfaction of the Court. Therefore, the party who wishes the Court to believe in the existence of a fact, must prove it. Whether a, witness should or should not be believed is one of peculiar difficulty owing to perjury that pervades the atmosphere of Courts in the country. Questions as to what a Court to do on this particular point can never be solved by any artificial rules of evidence or procedure as argued by Mr. Mahmudul Islam, and the best guide of a Court on such questions is its common sense and experience of human nature. Facts which are neither admitted nor are subject to judicial notice must he proved. The Evidence Act attaches more importance to the quantity than to the quality of evidence by providing that no number of the witnesses is in any case required for the proof of any fact. Proof of a fact would depend upon the character of the witness and his competency to speak to that fact.

23. In Sardar Gurbakhsh Singh V. Gurdial Singh and another, AIR 1927 P.C. 230 cited by Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the question involved was as to the legitimacy of a boy who is said to be the son of Bhagwan Kuar, younger wife of late Sardar Jawala Singh. The elder wife was childless, the younger has home to him a daughter, who according to the law did no inherit the estate. Bhagwan Kuar claimed the boy as her posthumous son to inherit the estate. Almost immediately after the death of her husband, Bhagwan disappeared. Bhagwan did not appear as a witness in the suit and her non appearance in answer to the legitimacy of her son, that is to say, to disclose the actual fact as to her condition shortly after husband's death and her disappearance was raised by her opponent. Their Lordships disbelieved the legitimacy of her alleged son on the view that she was purposely keeping out of the way. It was observed that this "would he the strongest possible circumstances going to discredit the truth of her 'case".  It was further observed "The true object to he achieved by a Court of justice can only be furthered with propriety by testimony of the party  who personally knowing the whole circumstances of the case can dispel the suspicious attaching to it. The story can then he subjected in all its particulars to cross-examination". The decision, in my humble opinion, instead of supporting the plaintiff's case supports the defendant's Case.

24. Though P.W.2 is a witness to the agreement for sale, the defendant had instituted a criminal case against him and P.W.5 in respect of the suit lands for criminal trespass and other related offences as will he evident from ext- 'Umo' a compromise petition filed in Siddir Ganj RS. Case No.7(11)/93 corresponding to G.R. Case No.309 of 1993. This exhibit sufficiently suggested that there was admitted enmity between the defendant and P.Ws.2 anti 5 over the suit lands. Even if the recitals in ext-'Umo' are not taken into consideration this document proves the enmity between them over the suit lands. In a case where enmity is admitted it is required as a rule of produce that there should he corroboration of the evidence of such interested witnesses as may inspire confidence in the mind or the Court as to the truth of the fact stated by them. P.Ws.3 and 4 are not witnesses of the transaction dated 27th March, 1984, and did not support the plaintiffs case that on the day of execution of the deed of agreement for sale the plaintiff was given possession of the suit lands. They deposed about the plaintiffs possession after the execution and registration of the sale deed. P.W.3 also did not say that the plaintiff had been possessing the suit land through P.W.2, whereas, P.W.2 stated that he was cultivating the suit land on behalf of the plaintiff. In Cross examination P.W.3 expressed his ignorance about the boundary of the suit lands. P.W.4 claimed that P.W.2 was cultivating the suit land as borgader of the plaintiff. In course of cross-examination, he could not say the plot numbers and the area of the suit lands and also could not say over whose property the parties were litigating. He admitted that there was a criminal case over dismantling of houses but he could not say who dismantled the house. There is total non-consideration of the above inconsistencies in the evidence of P.Ws.2-4.

25. The High Court Division affirmed the observations of the trial Court that PW.4 is a neutral witness on a superficial consideration of his testimony that he had no idea about the suit lands. These PWs.3 and 4 being not present at the time of execution the agreement for sale and non-appearance of the plaintiff and Akkas Ali without any explanation whatsoever sufficiently supports the submission of Mr. Bhuiyan that there is practically no reliable evidence in support of the plaintiffs case that he got possession on the date of execution of the agreement. The High Court Division being the final Court of fact ought to have assessed the evidence minutely but it has totally shirked its responsibilities as if it were disposing of a revision petition.

26. Besides ext-Cha and the averments in the plaint, the defendant has relied upon ext-Ka, the writ of delivery of possession and ext-Kha, the order of the Court confirming the delivery of possession in Title Execution Case No.40 of 1989, ext-Ga the order of the High Court Division in Civil Order No.1548 of 1993 in support of the defendant's possession. He also examined D.Ws.1-4 in support of his possession.

27. D.W.2 stated that he was a borgader and that the defendant had two houses on the suit land. The plaintiff did not challenge this statement. D.Ws.3 and 4 claimed as tenants under the defendant. These witnesses corroborated the evidence of D.W.1 about his possession in the suit lands. The learned Judges of the High Court Division disbelieved D.Ws.3 and 4 on the reasoning’s that they are chance witnesses. The learned Judges have not assigned any reason as to why they discarded the evidence of D.Ws.3 and 4 treating them as chance witnesses. Learned Judges believed the plaintiffs possession on the reasoning’s that D.Ws.6 and 8 being defendant's witnesses supported the plaintiffs possession. This finding is totally based on misreading the evidence of D.Ws.6 and 8. The manner in which the learned Judges discarded their evidence is deprecated. Nurul Islam (D.W.6) has been claiming the suit lands independently and contesting the suit as defendant No.7. He does not support the plaintiff or the defendant's case. Ramiz Uddin Mia (D.W.8) deposed in support of the case of the defendant No.7. Mr. Mahmudul Islam frankly concedes that the High Court Division on misreading the evidence of D.Ws.6 and 8 observed that they supported the plaintiffs possession.

28. Exhibit-Ga, the order of the High Court Division in Civil Order No.1548 of 1993 proved that the plaintiff had knowledge about the pendency of the execution case for effecting the delivery of possession of the suit lands to the plaintiff. Eat-'Ka' is the warrant of delivery of possession. The learned Subordinate Judge observed that the defendant by securing a collusive decree in Title Suit No.14 of 1986 and a collusive report from the process server by practicing fraud upon the Court, obtained the order of delivery of possession in Execution Case No.40 of 1989. These findings are based upon the solitary evidence of D.W.5, who has got admitted enmity with defendant. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, on the other hand, observed that if the defendant got the possession on 24th April, 1984, there was no reason on his part to take possession again through Court. These observations are based on surmises, inasmuch as, there is no iota of evidence or any finding that the defendant collusively obtained decree in Title Suit No.14 of 1986. As observed above, the plaintiffs predecessor had knowledge about the institution of the suit and filed a written statement and the plaintiff had also knowledge about the delivery of possession of the suit lands to the defendant through Court. There is practically no legal evidence in support of the findings of securing the collusive decree or possession   or the deed.

29. A general allegation of collusion implying some kind of fraud is not enough without particulars. Specific pleadings in support of fraud or collusion as per Order 6 Rule 4 are required to be made and those allegations of fraud and collusion must be substantially proved by the party making them. As regards the observation of the High Court Division that if the defendant got possession of the suit land on 24th April, 1984, there was no reason on his part to take possession through Court, Mr. Bhuiyan contended that as the defendant's possession was disturbed by D.Ws.2 and 5, a decree in a suit for specific performance   being executable, the defendant in order to ensure his possession perfect took the formal delivery of possession through Court so that the plaintiff could not disturb his possession. This submission of the learned Counsel can not be said to have no foundation at all. The learned Judges of the High Court Division failed to consider this aspect of the matter.

30. Now turning to the contention of Mr. Mahmudul Islam regarding illustrations (g) and (h) of Section 3 of the Specific Relief Act, it would be pertinent to keep in mind that these two illustrations are simple examples of a very intricate subject in equity. Notice required by the illustrations are two fold, either actual as in illustration (g), or constructive, that is, arising by operation of law, as in illustration (h). But the doctrine of notice in both cases is applicable to a two fold and converse class of cases; either it may be applied as in both these illustrations, to postpone or defeat a subsequent purchaser or incumbrance taking with notice, and to convert him into a trustee for the holder of some prior interest or it may be applied to protect one whose interest is subsequent in point of time, but who is a bonafide purchaser for valuable consideration without notice of some pre-existing interest. In the facts of the given case as discussed above, there is nothing on record to show that the defendant had knowledge about the plaintiffs possession pursuant to a previous agreement for sale with the vendors, rather it has been found that the plaintiff has the knowledge about the defendant's prior agreement for sale of the suit lands, his possession and the pendency of the execution proceeding for giving delivery of possession to the defendant. These facts proved that the plaintiff, collusively entered into an agreement for purchase of the suit lands with the vendors by creating an ante-dated agreement. After scanning the materials on record we are of the view that these illustrations can be applied against the plaintiff, not against the defendant.

31. What is more, admittedly the defendant obtained possession of the suit land in execution of the decree in Title Execution Case No.40 of 1989 and though the plaintiff alleged that this possession was collusive but he failed to substantiate his claim. The learned Subordinate Judge declared the deed as void but did not set aside the decree passed in Title Suit No.14 of 1986. Therefore, the decree still remains a valid one unless it is set aside or varied or annulled by a competent Court, the learned Subordinate Judge can not pass a decree declaring the deed void. The decree is totally an infructuous decree but the High Court Division has overlooked this vital point. The plaintiff ought to have filed a cross objection in the High Court Division under Order 41 Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the plaintiff remained satisfied with the decree. The High Court Division, in the premises, committed the fundamental error in maintaining an infructuous decree. If the decree is not set aside how can a Court invalidate and/or cancel a deed which has been registered in pursuance of the decree is not known to us?

32. The plaintiff though prayed for further relief but the Court did not pass such relief. The words further relief are meant not any and every kind of relief but one which would complete the claim of the plaintiff and not to lead to a multiplicity of suits. That further relief must flow necessarily from the relief of declaration. What is contemplated is a relief arising from the cause of action on which the plaintiffs suit is based. The relief which is inherent in original declaration claimed relief without which declaratory decree claimed would be meaningless and infructuous. Mr. Mahmudul Islam frankly concedes that the trial Court ought to have set aside the decree passed in Title Suit No.14 of 1986 but according to him that would not materially affect the decree passed by the trial Court. According to the learned Counsel, this is a mere technical defect and this Court can pass an effective decree modifying that of the trial Court since the plaintiff has been able to prove the suit, under Order 41 Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

33. It appeared that the plaintiff had sought for a declaration that the decree passed in Title Suit No.14 of 1986 to be declared illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff, but the learned Subordinate Judge did not pass any decree in that regard. There is no doubt that the terms of Rule 33 of Order 41 are very wide and in appropriate cases the appellate Court has ample discretion to pass any decree or make any order to prevent the ends of justice being defeated. Whether this power should be exercised would no doubt depend upon the special facts and circumstances of a particular case. Those powers are to be used only where equities between the parties have to be adjusted in a case where either the appeal is against part of the decree or by some out of persons affected by the trial Court's decree. If the appellate Court is of the view that any decree which ought in law to have been passed, but in fact not passed by the trial Court, it may pass or make such further order or other decree as the justice of the case may require. When the appellate Court finds inconsistent, contradictory or unworkable order it is in that case alone the appellate Court would exercise its power Order 41 Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure and not otherwise. We are of the view that the plaintiff without filing a cross-objection and attacking the decree of the trial Court by taking specific ground is not entitled to get the relief of setting aside the decree under Order 41 rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In view of the discussions made above, we find no merit in the contention of Mr. Mahmudul Islam.

34. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as, to cost. The suit is dismissed.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 11.03.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4245 of 2008)
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J.:- This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 11.03.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4245 of 2008 making the rule absolute, setting aside the judgment and order dated 13.08.2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 199 of 2008 summarily rejecting the revision thereby affirming the judgment and order dated 07.05.2008 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 2006 under section 4 of the Partition Act dismissing the case.

<u>2. The facts necessary for disposal of this Civil appeal, in short, are that one Kala Miah was the owner of the property in question. Kala Miah died leaving two wives, 8 sons and 10 daughters. From these heirs of Kala Miah the present respondent Kamrun Naher Begum purchased 2 anas 3 godans and 13 till share and the present appellants purchased the rest 13 anans 16 gondas,3 koras, 2 kranties, 7 till share. Kamrun Nahar Begum-the respondent herein-filed Partition Suit No. 86 of 1993 for declaration of title and for partition of her share in the suit property and get a decree on 04.06.2003. In that decree the present appellants also were allotted separate shaham for the rest 13 anas 16 gondas, 3 karas, 2 kranties, 7 til share. The said judgment and decree was upheld upto the High Court Division. Thereafter, the plaintiff of that Title Suit No. 86 of 1993 (the respondent herein) filed Miscellaneous Case No. 26 of 2006 for buying up the share of the opposite parties (the present appellants) under section 4 of the Partition Act contending, inter-alia, that the property in question was her homestead property and she had been possessing the same with her family members since 1978; that the opposite parties are stranger purchasers and they had no possession in this property. That the petitioner had been possessing the entire property on paying rent, municipal taxes, electricity, WASA and gas bills. The opposite parties are strangers and as such the petitioner was entitled to by up the share of the opposite parties and she was ready to pay the compensation money.</u>

3. The opposite party Nos. 1 to 3 contested the case by filing written statement contending, inter-alia, that they acquired the major share of about 14 annas in the property in question by three documents dated 30.04.1981 which was earlier then the purchase of the petitioner. That these opposite parties earlier filed Miscellaneous Case Nos. 189 and 190 of 1984 for preemption of the land of the petitioner and it went upto Appellate Division and the Appellate Division found that the property fell within Dhanmondi Residential Area and for this reason the pre-emption would not lie.

4. The trial court, on consideration of evidence adduced by both the parties and the facts and circumstances dismissed that miscellaneous case under section 4 of the Partition Act finding that the petitioner was not a member of undivided family and heir of Kala Miah and that she was a stranger purchaser and her purchase was subsequent to the purchase of the contesting opposite parties who were major share holders. The revisional court below affirmed this judgment of the trial court. The High Court Division set aside the concurrent findings and decision of the courts below and allowed the miscellaneous case by its impugned judgment and order.

5. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned senior Counsel appearing for the appellants has made submissions to the effect that admittedly the petitioner-respondent was not heirs of Kala Miah nor was a member of the family of Kala Miah, but she, admittedly became co-share by virtue of purchase from the heirs of Kala Miah. The learned Counsel has argued that both the courts of facts, on proper appreciation of these facts and circumstances rightly dismissed the case under section 4 of the Partition Act, but the High Court Division without adverting to or reversing the concurrent findings and decision of the courts below most unjustly allowed the case under section 4 of the Partition Act ignoring the fact that none of the elements for attracting operation of section 4 of the Partition Act was present in this case. The learned Counsel has argued that in this case it is an admitted fact that all the members of Kala Miah the original owner have transferred their entire interest in favour of the petitioner and the respondents and now there is no question of undivided family and that the petitioner, admittedly, being brother's daughter of one of the wives of Kala Miah is not a member of Kala Miah's family and that there is no evidence at all to prove that the petitioner was a member of Kala Miah's family. The learned Counsel has contended that the High Court Division most unreasonably and unjustly allowed this miscellaneous case under section 4 of the Partition Act by the impugned judgment and order and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside.

6. Mr. Mahbubey Alam and Mr. M. A. Quayum, the learned Senior Advocates for the respondent has made submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. They have made submissions to the effect that the petitioner being brother's daughter of one of the wives of Kala Miah used to reside in the property in question with the family of Kala Miah and as such her claim under section 4 of the Partition Act cannot be brushed aside.

7. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, those of the revisional court below and the trail court and also the evidence on record.

8. Section 4 of the Partition Act provides:

"Where a share of a dwelling house belonging to an undivided family has been transferred to a persons who is not a member of such family and such transferee sues for partition, the Court shall, if any member of the family being a share-holder shall undertake to buy the share of such transferee, make a valuation of such share in such manner as it thinks fit and direct the sale of such share to such share-holder, and may give all necessary and proper directions in that behalf."

9. From the above quoted section 4 it is evident, that the elements which must co-exists in order to attract the operation of section 4 of the Partition Act are:

(i). that the dwelling house should belong to an undivided family,

(ii) that the share thereof should have been transferred to a person who is not a member of such family,

(iii) that the transferee should sue for partition.

10. Here, in the present case, the main element for attracting section 4 of the Partition Act is absent. There is no existence of any undivided family now, Admittedly, Kala Miah was the original owner and possessor of the property in question and he died leaving 2 wives, 8 sons and 10 daughters. Admittedly, all of these heirs of Kala Miah have transferred their entire share in the property in question. It is also an admitted fact that the present appellants purchased about 14 annas share of the property in question from the heirs of Kala Miah before the purchase of 2 annas, 3 gondas and 13 till share by the petitioner respondent Kamrun Nahar Begum. So, admittedly the appellants and opposite party are now owners of the entire property in question and none of these appellants and the opposite party is heir of Kala Miah. So, the question of undivided family now does not arise at all.

11. From the side of the petitioner-respondent though some arguments has been advanced to the effect that the petitioner being the brother's daughter of one of the wives of Kala Miah used to reside in the property in question with the family of Kala Miah and as such she should be treated as the member of family of Kala Miah, but this argument also is not acceptable at all. It might be that the petitioner-respondent Kamrun Nahar Begum used to reside in the house of Kala Miah with his family but where, admittedly, all the heirs of Kala Miah sold out their entire share in the suit property in question, that is the entire property to the petitioner-respondent and the appellants opposite parties, there remains no question of any undivided family now.

12. In this case, admittedly, the transferee appellants did not file any suit for partition, rather they, as earlier purchasers filed preemption cases to preempt the land purchased the petitioner-opposite party. So the other element for attracting the operation of section 4 of the Partition Act-that is the transferee should sue for partition-also is absent in this case.

13. Both the petitioner-respondent and the appellants were stranger purchasers and admittedly the appellants purchased their share before the purchase of the petitioner-respondent. In the circumstances the prayer of the petitioner-respondent for buying up the share of the appellant opposite parties is not entertain-able at all.

<u>14. It appears that the trail court, on-proper appreciation of all the facts and law rightly rejected the case under section 4 of the Partition Act. The revisional court below also, on proper appreciation of the facts and law rightly affirmed this judgment and order of the trial. But it appears that the High Court Division set aside these concurrent findings and decision of the courts below and allowed the case under section 4 of the Partition Act, on making findings to the effect that "the opposite parties are strangers of the suit premises and the petitioner is residing in the suit land." Evidently, the High Court Division committed serious wrong and illegality in allowing the case under section 4 of the Partition Act on the above findings. In a case under section 4 of Partition Act the possession of the parties is not at all a necessary factor to be considered. So, the allowance of the prayer for buy off on the ground that the petitioner is in possession of the property in question and the purchaser opposite parties are not in possession-has been most erroneous and illegal. It appears that the learned Judge of the High Court Division, in its impugned judgment, though has quoted section 4 of the Partition Act, but could not appreciate the true purport of this very section.</u>

15. However, from the above discussion, it is evident, that the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division cannot be sustained in law.

16. In the circumstances this appeal is allowed on contest without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and those of the courts below are hereby affirmed.

End.

full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J.:- This Civil Appeal by leave, at the instance of the plaintiff, is directed against the judgment and order dated 28.10.2001 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 685 of 1998 making the rule absolute and thereby setting aside the concurrent findings and decision of the trial court and the appellate court below and sending the suit back on remand to the trial court with directions to the plaintiff to make necessary amendment to the plaint seeking partition of the suit land and to implead brothers of Tahera Khatun as defendants and also to bring all the properties into hotchpotch.

2. The facts necessary for disposal of this civil appeal are as follows:-

3. The present plaintiff-appellant filed Title Suit No. 223 of 1985 in the court of Additional Assistant Judge, Sadar, Noakhali for permanent injunction. Her case, in short, was that the land in question measuring 10 decimals of plot No. 324 of Diara Khatian No. 86 of mouza Ramanandi belonged to Hossain Ahmed and Tahera Khatun in equal share. Their names were recorded in the Diara Khatian correctly. That Hossain Ahmed died leaving his wife Tahera Khatun, a daughter-plaintiff, a brother-the defendant No. 3 and a sister-the defendant No. 4. Thus Tahera Khatun inherited from her husband 02½  decimal of land, the plaintiff inherited 1¼ decimals of land, the defendant No. 3 inherited 1¼  decimals of land and the defendant No. 4 inherited 0 5/8  decimal of land from Hossain Ahmed. Tahera Khatun by a deed of heba-bil-ewaj transferred her 5 decimals of land along with other lands to the plaintiff in the year 1979. Thereafter Tahera Khatun died leaving plaintiff as her heir. Thus the plaintiff by inheritance and by dint of heba-bil-ewaj deed acquired total 81⁄8  decimals of land. That there was an amicable partition amongst the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 and through that amicable partition the defendant No. 4 got her 5⁄8  decimals of land to the south of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 got his 1¼  decimals of land to the north of the plaintiff and the plaintiff got her 8-1⁄8   decimals of land in the middle and thus the plaintiff and the defendants were in possession of their respective share peacefully. That the plaintiff has huts in her share and she let out those to the tenants. The defendants threatened to dispossess the plaintiff from her share and thus the plaintiff was compelled to file the suit for permanent injunction.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1, and 4 by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter-alia, that the land measuring 10 decimals of plot No. 324 of Diara Khatian No. 86 of mouza Ramanandi belonged to Hossain Ahmed only. That Hossain Ahmed while in possession of these 10 decimals of land died leaving Tahera Khatun as wife, the plaintiff as daughter, the defendant No. 3 as brother and the defendant No. 4 as sister and thus Taher Khatun got 1¼ decimals in her 1⁄8 share, plaintiff got 5 decimals, defendant No. 3 got 1¼  decimals and defendant No. 4 got 1¼ decimals. That the defendant No. 1 is son of defendant No. 4 and he has been residing with his mother in the same mess in the suit land. That the defendant No. 4 filled up the ditch situated in the middle of suit plot about 15 years before and thereafter, the defendant No. 1 built চৌচালা but facing east thereon and also built another hut in the back of that চৌচালা hut and let out those to one Kala Miah who runs a tea shop therein. That to the south of the said shop there is the but of জলা সমিতি that the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 are possessing the land of this plot to the north of the but of the defendant Nos. 1 and 4. It is also the case of the contesting defendants that the suit land is vague and unspecified and that the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 being co-sharers the suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable.

5. Both these contesting parties adduced several witnesses before the court to prove their respective case.

6. The trial court, on consideration of evidence adduced by both the parties decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff has got right, title and possession in 8-1⁄8  decimals of land and that the suit land is well specified. Against the judgment of the trial court the contesting defendants went on appeal before the court of the learned District Judge, Noakhali and the said appeal was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali. The appellate court, on hearing both the parties and consideration of the evidence on record, dismissed that appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial court. The contesting defendants then filed the above mentioned Civil Revision No. 685 of 1998 before the High Court Division and obtained rule. Ultimately a Single Bench of the High Court Division, after hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties, made that rule absolute, set aside the concurrent findings and decision of the trial court and the appellate court below and sent back the suit on remand with the directions already mentioned above.

7. Mr. Nikhilesh Datta, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant has made submissions before us to the effect that both the trial court and the appellate court below, on proper examination and appreciation of the evidence adduced by both the parties concurrently found that the plaintiff has title in her claimed 8-1/8 decimals of land and she has also proved her exclusive possession therein by adducing sufficient evidence and found also that this claimed land of the plaintiff has been well specified and thus decreed the suit for permanent injunction rightly. The learned Advocate has argued that the High Court Division sitting in its revisional jurisdiction fell into error in setting aside the concurrent finding of facts of the courts below without assigning any tangible reasons. The learned Advocate has argued also that the evidence adduced by the defendants also has proved the plaintiff's case that she is in possession of her share in the middle part of the suit plot as described in the schedule to the plaint. The learned Advocate has argued also that the High Court Division in the circumstances committed illegality and also injustice in sending back the case on remand for retrial after converting the suit into a partition suit by making necessary amendments and bringing all other common lands of the parties in the hotchpotch of the suit and impleading other co-shares. The learned Advocate has contended that it is well settled that a co-share in exclusive possession, even if, in excess of his/her actual share, can maintain her possession until partition and as such a suit for permanent injunction by such co-sharer is maintainable. The learned Advocate has contended that the High Court Division without considering this legal aspect set aside the concurrent findings and decision of the court below and most unjustly sent back the suit on remand causing much sufferings to this plaintiff-appellant.

8. Mr. N. 1. Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate-on-Record for the defendant-respondents has made some submissions to the effect that in this suit the plaintiff could not prove her exclusive possession in the suit land and that the suit land also is not well specified and in the circumstances the High Court Division rightly sent back the suit on remand with the direction to convert the suit into a partition suit by bringing necessary amendments to the plaint.

9. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment, those of the appellate court below and the trial court and also the evidence on record.

10. Admittedly, 10 decimals land of plot No. 324 of mouza Ramanandi has been recorded in Diara Khatian No. 86 in the name of Hossain Ahmed and his wife Tahera Khatun in equal share. The plaintiffs case is that Hossain Ahmed and Tahera Khatun were the owners of these 10 decimals of land in equal share. But the contesting defendant's case is that Hossain Ahmed was the owner of these 10 decimals of land and that the name of Tahera Khatun was recorded in the Diara Khatian wrongly. But it appears that the courts below did not accept this case of the contesting defendants in view of the evidence and the facts and circumstances on record. This Diara Khatain was prepared long before. The own witness of the contesting defendants also has admitted that this Diara Khatian No. 86 of mouza Ramanandi was prepared long before during the life time of Hossain Ahmed. Admittedly neither Hossain Ahmed nor any of his heirs ever raised any objection against this Diara Khatian No. 86. Rather it appears that Tahera Khatun transferred 5 decimals of land to her daughter-the plaintiff by registered heba-bil-ewaj deed in the year 1979. But none of the heirs of Hossain Ahmed has ever raised any question anywhere as to this registered heba-bil-ewaj deed executed by Tahera Khatun in respect of 5 decimals land of suit plot in favour of the plaintiff. Considering all these facts and circumstances the courts below rightly found that the land in question; i.e. 10 decimals land of plot No. 324 originally belonged to Hossain Ahmed and Tahera Khatun in equal share. So, the plaintiff Noor Jahan Begum acquired total 8 and 1⁄8  decimals of land both by virtue of inheritance from her father Hossain Ahmed and Mother Tahera Khatun and also by a registered heba-bil-ewaj deed of the year 1979 from Tahera Khatun. The plaintiff has claimed that there has been amicable partition amongst the co-sharers of the land of suit plot, namely, the plaintiff herself and the defendant Nos. 3 and 4 and by that amicable partition she got her share of 814 decimals of land in the middle portion of the suit plot and the defendant No. 4 got 5⁄8  decimals of land to the south of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 3 got 1¼ decimals of land to the north of the plaintiff and since that amicable partition the plaintiff has been possessing her 8 and 5⁄8 decimals of land in the middle portion of the suit plot peacefully.

11. The plaintiff adduced as many as 5 witnesses to prove her possession in the suit land. On the other hand the contesting defendants also have examined 4 witnesses to prove their case.

12. We have examined the evidence adduced by both the parties.

13. The P.W.1 Md. Shahan Uddin is the son of the plaintiff. He has deposed before the court in support of the plaint case. He has specifically stated that through amicable partition the plaintiff has been possessing 81⁄(8 )decimals of land in the middle of the suit plot and the defendant No.4 has been possessing her 5⁄8 decimals of land to the south of the plaintiff and the defendant No.3 has been possessing his 1¼ decimals of land to the north of the plaintiff and that the plaintiffs have several huts on her share which she has been possessing by letting out to different tenants. The P.W. 2 Monu Miah is a common relation of both the contesting parties. This witness also has deposed before the court fully supporting the case of the plaintiff. He has deposed to the effect that the plaintiff is the owner in possession of 8 and 1⁄8 decimals of land of the suit plot and the defendant No. 4 is the owner in possession of 5⁄8  decimal of land and the defendant No. 3 is owner in possession of 1¼  decimals of land and that there has been an amicable partition among these owners of the suit property in his presence and through that amicable partition the plaintiff has been possessing his share in the middle of the suit plot while the defendant No. 3 has been possessing his share to the north of the plaintiff and the defendant No. 4 has been possessing her share to the south of the plaintiff and that the plaintiff has got several huts within her share. The P.W. 3 Abdul Sahid also has deposed to the effect that he has got his medicine shop near the suit land and that the plaintiff has been possessing 81⁄8 decimals of land in the middle of the suit plot and the defendant No. 3 has been possessing his 1¼ decimals of land to the north of the plaintiff and the defendant No.4 has been possessing her 1⁄4  decimals of land to the south of the plaintiff. This witness also has stated that there was an amicable partition of the suit property among the plaintiff and the defendants. The P.W. 4 Mafizullah also has deposed to the effect that the plaintiff has 3 huts in the middle of the suit plot and that the defendant No. 3 has been possessing on the northern portion of the suit plot while the defendant No. 4 has been possessing on the southern portion of the suit plot. This witness has stated also that he has rented two shops of the suit land from the plaintiff. The P.W. 5 Abdul Motaleb is another tenant of the plaintiff. This witness also has deposed to the effect that the plaintiff is in possession in the middle of the suit plot while the defendant No. 4 has been possessing in the southern part of the suit plot and the defendant No. 3 has been possessing in the northern part of the suit plot.

14. The contesting defendant No. 1 has deposed as D.W.1. He is the son of the defendant No. 4. This witness though has tried to disprove the plaintiffs case, but he has virtually admitted the plaintiffs possession in the suit plot by stating to the effect that "নালিশী দাগের ভূমিতে বাদীনির অংশে বাদীনির ঘর আছে। বাদীনি তাহার উক্ত ঘর ভাড়া দিয়া দখলে আছে।"

15. The D.W. 2 is the defendant No. 3. It appears that this witness has rather admit-ted the case of the plaintiff by stating to the effect that "নালিশী দাগের সর্ব উত্তরে আমি, তৎদক্ষিণে বাদীনি নুরজাহান, তৎদক্ষিণে ১নং বিবাদী গিয়াস উদ্দিন --------”

"These statements of the defendant No. 3-who has deposed as a witness of the contesting defendant Nos. 1 and 4-proves the plaintiffs case that she has possessed her share in the middle portion of the suit plot. These statements of this D.W. 2 have also disproved the case of the contesting defendant. This D.W. 2 has supported also the case of the plaintiff of amicable partition by stating to the effect that "বাদীনির পুত্রগণসহ আমার পূত্ররা নালিশী দাগের ভূমি/বন্টক করিয়া নিয়াছে।" The D.W.3 Harish Mia has deposed only to the effect that he is a tenant of a shop but under the defendant No. 1 and he has been running a tea stall therein and that the defendant No. 1 has got 2 huts in the lands of suit plots and that there are some vacant land to the west of these 2 huts which the defendant No. 1 has been possessing. Evidently, the deposition of this D.W. 3 is of no help for the contesting defendant. The D.W. 4 Elahi Box also has deposed supporting the plaintiff's case. This witness has stated to the effect that to the north of the defendant No. 1 the plaintiff has 3/4 kara land and that the plaintiff possessed there about 7½ decimals of land. The plaintiffs case also is that the defendant No. 4, mother of the defendant No. 1 has been possessing to her south and the defendant No. 3 has been possessing to her north. So, it appears that the evidence of this defendant's witness No. 4 also has supported the plaintiffs case.

<u>16. The trial court and the appellate court below, on proper consideration and appreciation of these evidence adduced by both the parties rightly found that the plaintiffs exclusive possession in her claimed 8 and 1⁄8 decimals of land has been well proved. We also, in agreement with the courts of facts, find that in this suit the evidence adduced by both the contesting parties has proved well that the plaintiff, an admitted co-sharer, has got exclusive possession in her claimed 8 and 1⁄8 decimals of land of the suit plot as described in the schedule to the plaint. This claimed land of the plaintiff has been well described in the schedule to the plaint by mentioning all the four boundaries. In the circumstances the trial court rightly decreed the suit for permanent injunction and the appellate court below rightly affirmed this judgment and decree of the trial court. It is well settled that a co-sharer in possession can maintain her possession until partition. A co-sharer in exclusive possession of land, even if, in excess of his/her actual share, cannot be dispossessed otherwise than by partition and hence a co-sharer in exclusive possession can bring a suit for permanent injunction against the other co-sharers-who threaten him/her with dispossession.</u>

<u>17. So, evidently the High Court Division was not justified at all to send back the suit on remand for fresh trial with the direction to convert the suit for permanent injunction into a suit for partition. In this suit the plaintiff-a co-sharer has proved her exclusive possession in her claimed land and she is entitled to keep this possession until partition by metes and bounds. If necessary, the defendants-co-sharers can bring a suit for partition, the plaintiff cannot be compelled to file a suit for partition.</u>

18. In the circumstances this appeal be allowed on contest without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aide and those of the trial court and the appellate court below are affirmed.

End.
