full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: <u>This is defendants' appeal by leave against the Judgment dated July 5, 1998 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No 2289 of 1992 making the Rule absolute obtained against the judgment and decree dated April 30, 1992 of the Court of Subordinate Judge and 1st Commercial Court, Chittagong in other Appeal No.301 of 1990 affirming the judgment and decree dated March 28, 1990 of the 1st Additional Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong, Sadar in other suit No. 12 of 1990 dismissing the same. The suit was filed seeking eviction of the licensee/ permissive possessor and for khan possession, of the land described in the schedule attached to the plaint.</u>

2. The suit was filed stating, inter alia, that the land in suit belonged to Yakub Ali Dobhash and others and they settled the land in suit on nominal rent to the plaintiff, J.M. Sen Institute, about 65 years back (from the date of institution of the suit i.e. 3.12.1987 and since then the school upon constructing house thereon was possessing the land so settled, that Genoda Ranjan chakraborty, the predecessor of the defendants was a clerk of the school and he was permitted to live in the premises in suit with the members of his family, that predecessor of the defendants having had died leaving the defendant No. 1 and the minor children defendant Nos. 2-4, and the defendant No. 1 having had approached the school authority for allowing them to stay in the premises for some time the school authority permitted the defendants to stay temporarily in the premises in suit , that defendant No.1, wife of Genoda Ranjan Chakraborty made commitment to the school authority that on attainment of majority of the defendant Nos. 2-4 she would leave the premises in suit, that on attainment of majority of the defendant Nos. 2-4 the school authority asked the defendants to vacate the premises in suit but instead of vacating the premises in suit the defendant No. 1 instituted other Suit No.83 of 1967 seeking a decree for permanent injunction against the school and obtained an order of ad-interim injunction making untrue averments, that the school authority on September 3, 1970 wrote a letter to the defendants asking them to leave the premises in suit and to deliver vacant possession in favour of the school but instead of vacating the premises in suit the defendants on different pleas continued their possession in the premises in suit and finally refused to vacate the premises in suit and hence the suit was filed on 3.12.1983.

3. The suit was contested by the defendants by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the suit was barred by limitation and that also hit by the provision of sections 10 and 11 of the code of Civil procedure. The specific ease of the defendants was that the land in suit belonged to Abdul Majid Dobhash son of Yakub Ali Dobhash and that R.S. khatian stood in his name, that defendants predecessor was the house tutor of the children of Abdul Majid Dobhash in between1920 and 1923, that Abdul Majid Dobhash being satisfied with the service of defendants Predecessor gifted the land in suit to defendants predecessor, that lateron in 1965 Abdul Majid Dobhash executed a deed of gift in favour of the defendants predecessor that the P.S. record was prepared in the name of the defendants that plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the land in suit and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit On the findings that the plaintiff failed to prove when cause of action arose for filing the suit, that the suit was barred by limitation since alter the institution of the other suit No. 83 of 1967 by the defendants the plaintiff has filed the suit in 1989, that the land of the patta and the land in suit is not the same, that it has not been established that land of Ext. 3(Ka) patta was the land of Yakub Ali and that on the basis of patta it can not be said that the plaintiff has title in the land in suit, that on the basis of the rent receipt Bled by the plaintiff title of the plaintiff can not be decided and on the basis of the rent receipt it can not be said that the plaintiff has title in the land in suit, that the plaintiff has not taken any step against the R. S. and P.S. khatian and that on the basis of the said khatians it can not be said that title of the plaintiff has been proved, that defendants in support of their claim have filed an unregistered deed of gift and p.s. khatian and that as the plaintiff has not taken any exception to the preparation of p.s. khatian in respect of the land in suit in the name of the defendants and as such it can be said that the defendants have title in the land in suit, that to prove the unregistered deed of gift Ext. ঙ. defendants have examined d.w. 2, the writer of the deed of gift, that plaintiffs have failed to prove that they have title in the land in suit and that because of the p.s. khatian defendants have title in the land in suit, that as the plaintiffs suit is barred by limitation and that plaintiff failed to prove its case and as such the question of defendants stay on the land in suit as permissive possessor is redundant, that the plaintiffs suit is hit by the provision of section 10 of the Code of Civil procedure since other Class Suit No.83 of 1967 filed by the defendants is still pending, that plaintiffs suit as framed is not maintainable.

5. As against the judgment and decree of the trial Court the plaintiff went on appeal. The appellate Court upon the findings that plaintiff failed to produce and prove any document of title either in favour of itself or in the name of Yakub Ali Dobhash and as against that defendants proved that the land originally belonged to Abdul Majid Dobhash and the R. S. and P.S. Khatian was prepared in his name and the P.S. Khatian has been prepared in the name of the defendant No.1, that plaintiff has not challenged the khatian prepared in the name of Abdul Majid Dobhash and in the name of defendant No.1 and as such correctness those of remain unrebutted and that the defendants in support of their claim in the land in suit have produced the deed of gift Ext. 'uma' ( brought on record through the evidence of D.W.2, claimed to be the writer of the deed which is not a registered one), that cause of action for filing the suit by the plaintiff arose prior to the filing of the other class suit No.83 of 1967 by the defendants and as such plaintiffs suit is barred under sections 11 and 10 of the Code of Civil procedure since the suit, i.e. other class suit No.83 of 1967 filed by the defendants is pending. The appellate court also held that the suit was barred by limitation since the same was file "after a long period of 20 years" i.e. from 1967, that from the perusal of the memorandum of appeal it appears that the appellant did not specifically made out any case for interfering   with the judgment of the trial court and that memorandum of appeal also does not disclose in which respect the trial court was in error or committed illegality and thereupon holding that the judgment and decree of the trial court does not call for interference dismissed the appeal.

6. The plaintiff moved the High court division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division on consideration of materials on record observed that the courts below upon wrong assumption of fact and law have held that the suit was barred under the provision of section 11 of the code of civil procedure and that the suit was also barred by limitation since the suit was not filed in 1967 when the cause of action first arose on the institution of the other class suit No.83 of 1967 filed by the defendants seeking a decree for permanent injunction and obtained an order of temporary injunction therein, that the decision made by the courts below that the suit was barred under section 11 of the code of civil procedure was totally misconceived since the question of permissive possession of the defendants on the date of institution of the suit filed by the plaintiff was not an issue in any suit and that was not finally adjudicated between the parties in the suit filed by the plaintiff, that from the defendants' side no paper relating to the claim of possession acquired otherwise then by permission granted by the plaintiff was placed before the Court , that the decision of the courts below that the suit was barred by limitation is not sustainable in law as "in a suit for ejectment of a licensee, the question to be firstly determined whether the defendant is a licensee or permissive possessor under the plaintiff, if that is established, the question of limitation will not arise at all because a licensee occupies the property according to the pleasure of the licensor and that occupation does not confer upon the right of exclusive possession as under-stood in law", that the appellate court on the misconception of the law and the issue involved in the suit and that upon misappreciation of the issue involved in the suit dismissed the appeal, that plaintiff proved his title in the land in suit and that also proved the case that the defendants are the licensees of the plaintiff upon production of the "documents of the title and the paper showing proof of possession by Ext.1 series, Exts. 5, 6 and 7 and also proved the applications addressed to the school authority by the defendant No.1, which were marked Exts.9 and 9(ka) indicated that the husband of the defendant No.1 has been staying as permissive possessor or as licensee in the suit premises" Ext. 1 series arc the R.S. Khatians, Ext.2-P.S. Khatians, Exts.3 and 3(ka) patta, Ext. 5- Municipal Assessment Register, Ext.6, 1 Municipal Tax receipt, Ext. 7 Rent receipt issued by the Government, Exts. 9 and 9(ka) dated 25.3.1967 and 25.1.1967 respectively applications filed by the defendant No.1 to the school authority seeking time for vacating the premises in suit.

7. The High Court Division observed that the courts below have not considered the Exts.9 and 9(ka) "to arrive at a finding i whether the defendants are a licensee under the plaintiff or they are in possession of the premises otherwise then licensee", that PS. khatian stood in the name of the school and "There is no contrary evidence that the defendants acquired their right in the suit premises otherwise then the grant made by the plaintiff, inasmuch as their claim in the written statements that the suit premises was gifted by the previous owner to the predecessor of the defendants has not been proved by any admissible evidence", that from the perusal of the Exts. 9 and 9(ka) and Ext. 10 (letter written by the plaintiff to the defendants to leave the premises in suit), it is seen that the defendants are permissive possessor or licensee in the suit premises and this material aspect was not considered by the courts below that one who is mere licensee, license so granted is without any other right is revocable at any time at the will of the licensor and that there is no provision in the Limitation Act providing limitation for filing a suit within specified time, that in view of the provision of section 116 of the Evidence Act licensee is incompetent to question the title of the licensor, that the finding of the courts below that the suit was barred by limitation and that plaintiff was not able to prove a " good title is totally misconceived and cannot be maintained", that licensee is not competent to take a plea of adverse possession, that "the possession of the plaintiff school having been established by various documentary evidence as well as the oral evidence and therefore, under the equitable rule of law, the defendants who were given permission to occupy the suit premises by the original person in possession that is the plaintiff school, cannot say that the plaintiff has no title to the subject matter of the contention urged by the learned Advocate of the opposite party does not stand" On the aforesaid observations and findings the High court Division made the Rule absolute.

8. Leave was granted to consider the contention that Exts. 9 and 9(ka) having not been proved in accordance with law arc inadmissible in evidence and that there having no other evidence in proof of licensee status of the defendants, the High court Division fallen into an error of law in holding that the defendants are licensees under the plaintiff, that it was inappropriate for the High court Division to give an independent decision on the facts over which both the courts were silent and in that state of the matter the High Court Division was required to send back the case on remand for decision on the point.

9. It appears the last contention has been made as regard the Exts. 9 and 9(ka) i.e. the applications filed by the defendant No.1 on the death of her husband for allowing them to stay on the land in suit for some time with the averment that they would vacate the land in suit within the time, if allowed. It also appears the school i.e. plaintiff allowed time but instead of vacating the premises in suit they filed suit No. 83 of 1967 seeking a decree for permanent injunction.

10. It is seen from the materials on record the school authority is claiming the land on the basis of the patta of June 27, 1912 and August 24, 1938. The plaintiff in support of title filed the sight plan of the school which was marked as Ext.4, copy of the municipal assessment register Ext. 5, municipal tax receipts (2) Ext.6 series, rent receipts (2) Ext.7 series, notice of the municipality relating to tax matter (Ext.8), Exts.9 and 9(Ka), applications of the defendant No. 1 seeking time, letter of the school authority of July 20, 1969 to the defendant No.1, Ext. 10 and the notice dated 3.9.1970 to the defendant No.1 by the school. As against the said documents of the plaintiff in support of its title in the land in suit defendants case was that the land in suit was gifted to their predecessor Genoda Ranjan Chakraborty, who according to the defendants was a teacher of the school but according to the plaintiff i.e. school was a clerk, by Abdul Majid Dobhash. The gift to defendants predecessor it appears initially was an oral gift and later on a memorandum of gift was prepared mentioning name of Abdul Majid Dobhash. There is nothing in the pleading if the defendants or in the deposition of the defendant No.2 in which Year Abdul Majid Dobhash orally Gifted the property being satisfied to Genoda Ranjan Chakraborty, who claimed to have been a house tutor of the children of Abdul Majid Dobhash, some time in between 1925 and 1930.

11. It may by mentioned there is no reliable evidence on record to support the defendants' ease of gift by Abdul Majid Dobhash while their predecessor was a house tutor of the children of said Abdul Majid Dobhash. As stated hereinbefore the plaintiff is claiming the land on the basis of the patta of the year 1912 and 1938. 'the defendants as observed by the trial court and the lower appellate court that in proof of their case filed the Ext. 'Uma' i.e. memorandum of gift (not registered) and tried to prove the said memorandum of gift through the evidence of D.W.2 D.W. 2 deposed on March, 1990. The witness has stated that he wrote the unregistered deed of gift by Abdul Majid Dobhash and he wrote the said memorandum of gift on the dictation of the donor i.e. Abdul Majid Dobhash. The witness in his cross examination has stated that at the time of writing the deed of gift in 1965 certain khidir Babu, Dhirandra, Abdul Majid Dobhash and Majid Hawlader were present and they are alive. The witness has stated that he for the first time new Abdul Majid Dobhash on the date of writing the deed of gift, The deposition of this witness has not been corroborated by any other independent and competent witness. It may be mentioned persons, including Abdul Majid Dobhash who said to have gifted the property to the defendants' predecessor, who were present as stated by D.W.2, at the time of writing the deed of gift were alive but none of them were examined by the defendants without offering any explanation. Abdul Majid Dobhash was the son of Yakub Ali Dobhash and Yakub Ali Dobhash gifted the property in suit to the school in 1992. The p.s. Khatian in respect of the land wherein the school situates and part of which is the subject matter of the suit is in the name of the school and the school is paying rent as evidenced by Ext.7 Series.

12. It appears from the judgment of the court of appeal below and the court of first instance that p.s. Khatian has been prepared in the name of the defendants as regard the land in suit but the said courts were quite oblivious of the fact that there was no basis for the preparation of the p.s. Khatian in the name of the defendants in respect of the land is suit. The trial court as well as the appellate court did not at all consider the vital evidence Exts.9 and 9(ka) which were filed by the defendant No.1 seeking time for vacating the land is suit. Although defendant No.2 who figured as D. W.1 has denied that the signature appearing in the said Exhibits were not of his mother but defendant No.1 herself has not come before the Court to deny the fact of filing of the said applications i.e. Exts.9 and 9(ka) and to say that the signatures appearing in the Exts.9 and 9(ka) are not of her. The said Exhibits have come from the custody of the proper and competent authority i.e. from the custody of the school. The said Exhibits were also put into evidence through the competent witness i.e. p.w.1, Head Master of the school and Secretary of the school in whose custody the papers were.

13. The court of appeal below as well as the court of first instance in discarding the case of the plaintiff that the defendants were the licensees of the plaintiff did not at all consider the Exts.9 and 9(ka) which demolished the claim of the defendants that they were and are not the licensees of the school. In this background of the fact the High Court Division was quite correct in holding that the judgments of the court of appeal below and of the trial court were based on misconception of the law involved in the case and plaintiffs suit was dismissed on non-consideration of the material evidence. The defendants claimed that the land was gifted to their predecessor in between 1925 and 1930 by Abdul Majid Dobhash and that lateron by the Ext. 'Uma' in 1965 Abdul Majid Dobhash gifted the land by a deed of gift. At no point of time defendants have paid rent to the landlord or to the Government of Bangladesh and that no tax or levy was paid to the municipal authority and that no municipal holding was opened in the name of the defendants' predecessor or in the name of the defendants in respect of the land in suit. On the other hand the plaintiff has filed the papers to show that the municipal holding stand in the name of the school and the school is paying rent and that municipality issued letter in the name of the school for the rent of the holding and that the school has paid rent to the Government in respect of the land in suit.

<u>14. In our view in the background of the aforesaid facts the court of appeal below and the trial court were in serious error in holding that the plaintiff failed to prove its title and possession in the land in suit. The trial court as well as lower appellate court held that the suit was barred as per provision of sections 10 and 11 of the code of civil procedure because of the pendency of the other class suit No.83 of 1967 which was filed by the defendants seeking for a decree of permanent injunction and still pending. The trial court as well as the appellate court were quite unmindful of the fact that in a suit for permanent injunction title of the parties is not adjudicated. The trial court as well as the appellate court was also in error in holding that the suit was barred under section 11 of the code of civil procedure since the subject matter of the suits i.e. other class suit No. 12 of 1990 filed by the plaintiff and the other class suit No. 83 of 1967 was not the same and the issues involved in the suits are also not the same. The trial Court as well as the appellate court was of the view that the suit was barred by limitation since it was filed after long 20 years computing from 1967, i.e. the year in which the defendants filed the suit for permanent injunction, in that thereby the license that was granted by the plaintiff did stand revoked, in that regard view expressed by the high court Division and the decision made in our opinion is correct.</u>

15. In the background of the discussions made hereinabove we find no merit in the appeal.

16. Accordingly the appeal is dismissed.

17. There is no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: This petition for leave to appeal arises out of the judgment dated 9.3.2005 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4369 of 1998 discharging the Rule which was obtained against the judgment and decree dated 24.6.1998 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Small Causes Courts, Brahmanbaria in S.C.C. Suit No. 02 of 1993 decreeing the suit.

<u>2. Sayeda Hosena Khatun, the predecessor of the respondent Nos. 1(a) and 1(b), instituted the above suit praying for ejectment of the defendants from the suit premises and also recovery of khas possession of the same stating, inter alia, that her husband Syed Nurul Huda alias Elu Mia became the owner of the suit premises by purchasing the same from Syed Dudu Mir and Abu Mir, after his death she and her 1 son and 2 daughters became the owners of the suit land by inheritance; she inducted defendant Nos. 1 and 3 in suit premises as monthly ejectable tenants on the basis of two agreements; they, in violation of the agreements and without taking her consent sub let the suit premises in favour of defendant Nos.2, 4 and 5; then the defendant No.1 filed Title Suit No. 5 of 1998 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Akhaura, Brahmanbaria against the defendant No.3 including the defendant Nos. 2, 4 and 5 and also defendant Nos. 43, 56, 46, 48 and 63 for declaration of his title in the suit land which by judgment dated 29.9.1991 was decreed; as against that the above defendants filed Title Appeal No. 71 of 1991 which was dismissed for non-prosecution on 27.1.1992; the defendants are defaulters for non-payment of monthly rents; the plaintiff served notice up on the defendants under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act terminating the tenancy and asking them to vacate the suit premises but the defendants did not vacate and hence the suit.</u>

3. The defendant Nos. 3, 4 and 5 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit is barred by limitation; since bonafide dispute is involved regarding title and possession the suit is not maintainable in its present form, the defendants are also not tenants under the plaintiff; One Mohram Ali, was the original owner of the suit land measuring 57 decimals who died leaving 3 sons and 3 daughters as heirs; the defendants are the owners of the suit premises by purchase from Moharam Ali; the defendant No.1 died during pendency of the suit whose heirs have not yet been made parties in the suit by substitution; the judgment and decree dated 26.9.1991 passed in Title Suit No.5 of 1998 is not binding upon the defendants as no notice was served upon them; the plaintiff filed the present suit on some false plea and hence the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial court, after hearing, decreed the suit. As against that the defendants moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 4369 of 1998 and after hearing the High Court Division discharged the Rule.

5. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division did not consider that defendant Nos.2, 4 and 5 are not the tenants of the suit premises under the plaintiff and so the above suit for ejectment of the defendants, who are not tenants in the suit premises, is not maintainable; the High Court Division failed to notice that the defendants not being made parties in the Title Suit No.5 of 1988, the judgment and decree passed therein is not binding on them; the High Court Division erroneously found that the defendant Nos.2, 4 and 5 are sub-tenants in the suit premises and so they have no locus-standi to resist their eviction from the suit premises and moreover the High Court Division on wrong assumption found that contesting defendants have accepted all the assertions of the plaintiff as made in the plaint.

<u>6. As it appears the High Court Division discharged the Rule on consideration of the submission that the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 5 were parties to the earlier Title Suit No.5 of 1988 but they did not contest the said suit and accordingly the decree passed in the said suit declaring the title of the plaintiff in the suit land is binding on all the defendants; the clear case of the plaintiff is that the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 entered the suit premises as tenants under the plaintiff on the basis of agreements Ext.3 and 3(ka) and they paid rents but subsequently inducted defendant Nos.2, 4 and 5 as sub-tenants and/or permitted defendants Nos.2, 4 and 5 to conduct business in the suit premises without any consent of the plaintiff and this clear assertion of the plaintiff in the plaint was not denied or challenged by the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 though summons were served upon them and accordingly the above statements in the plaint, being undenied, stands admitted so far as the monthly tenancy of defendant Nos.1 and 3 under the plaintiff; in the plaint the plaintiff also clearly asserted that the defendant Nos.1 and 3, being the tenants under the plaintiff, sublet the suit premises in the form of granting permission to defendant Nos. 2, 4 and 5 to carry on business in the suit premises without any consent obtained in writing from the plaintiff; in the plaint it was further asserted that the plaintiff required the suit premises for rebuilding the same for his bonafide requirement; the above statements went uncontroverted by defendant Nos. 1 and 3 and thus the said statements also stand admitted; P.W.1, 2, 3 ,4 and 5 proved the plaintiffs case of subletting of the suit premises of defendant Nos. 2, 4 and 5 by defendant Nos. 1 and 3 without written consent of the plaintiff and the said witnesses also proved bonafide requirement of plaintiff of the suit premises for re-building the same; P.W.5 is the scribe of the agreements Ext.3 and 3(ka) as regards granting monthly tenancy by plaintiff in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 3; the finding of the trial court that in Title Suit No. 5 of 1988 the title of the plaintiff has been declared in presence of the defendant Nos. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 including sever-al others on the basis of decree dated 26.9.1991 is supported by the decree of the said suit, Ext. 1; P.Ws. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 in their deposition also categorically stated that the defendant Nos. 2, 4 and 5 were inducted by defendant Nos. 1 and 3 which show that the defendant Nos. 1 and 3, being the tenants under the plaintiff, sub-let the suit premises in favour of defendant Nos. 2, 4 and 5 by way of permitting them to carry on business in the suit premises without any consent of the landlord and so the defendants 2, 4 and 5 being sub-tenants in the suit premises have no locus-standi to resist their eviction from the suit premises.</u>

7. We are of the view that the High Court Division on proper consideration of the evidence and the materials on record arrived at a correct decision. The learned counsel could not point at any illegality or infirmity in the decision of the High Court Division so as to call for any interference.

8. The petition is dismissed.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 21.08.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2414 of 2008)
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana J.:- This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen from the judgment and order dated 21.08.2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2414 of 2008 making the rule absolute and setting aside the judgment and order dated 20.03.2008 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Civil Revision No. 93 of 2007 affirming the order dated 12.03.2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 95 of 1982 rejecting an application under sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The facts necessary for disposal of this civil appeal, in short, are that the present appellants instituted Title Suit No. 95 of 1982 in the 1st Court of the learned Joint District Judge, Dhaka against the present respondents and others for partition. The material case of the plaintiffs was that the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and the defendant No. 1 were full brothers and they jointly purchased 0.5Y2 acre land of C.S. Plot No. 164 of C.S. Khatian No. 6 of Mouza Ibrahimpur, Police Station-Tejgaon, Dhaka in equal shares by a registered deed dated 06.01.1964 from the original owners Joynab Ali and others and since purchase the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and the defendant No. 1 (the deceased father of the present respondent Nos. 1(a) to 1(d)) had been possessing the said land in ejmali. That the previous owners of the land of the suit plot subsequently sold out the entire land of the suit plot to the defendant Nos. 1 to 9 and thus the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 1 to 9 being co-sharers of the entered of the suit plot had been possessing the same in ejmali. That though the respective shares of all these co-sharers had not been demarcated as yet the defendant No. 1 started construction of a building in the suit plot encroaching more land than his actual share. The plaintiffs requested the defendant No. 1 for amicable partition, but the defendant No. 1 refused and thus the plaintiffs were compelled to file the suit for partition.

3. The defendant No. 1 appeared in that suit and filed written statement admitting the fact that he himself and the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 jointly purchased 0.51/2 acre land of the suit plot No. 164 from Joynab Ali and others by registered deed dated 06.01.1964. That the defendant No. 1 purchased other lands also of the suit plot jointly with other defendants. After the death of the defendant No. 1 his heirs-(the present respondent Nos. 1(a) to 1(d)) were substituted in his place as defendant Nos. (a) to (d). These defendants pleaded a case to the effect that the defendant No. 1(c) also acquired .02¼ acre of land of the suit plot by a registered heba-bil-ewaz deed dated 21.04.1999 and thus the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) owned and possessed total .06(117/120) acre of land in the suit plot. This defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) also prayed for separate saham for .06117/120 acre of land.

4. The trial court decreed the suit in preliminary form by the judgment and order dated 19.11.2002 allotting shaham for .03-2/3 acre of land to the plaintiffs and .06(117/120) acre of land to the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d). An Advocate Commissioner was ultimately appointed to effect partition between the parties as per the said preliminary decree and the said Advocate Commissioner submitted his report on 29.08.2005 which was accepted and thereafter the final decree was drawn up on 30.11.2005.

5. On 20.03.2006 the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) filed an application under sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for correction of the said final decree on the ground that the final decree was not drawn up in accordance with the preliminary decree and that the Advocate Commissioner allocated lands to the plaintiffs from the lands in possession of the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) wherein they have a multistoried building. The learned Joint District Judge, upon hearing both the parties, rejected the said application. The defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) preferred revision before the learned District Judge against that order of the learned Joint District Judge and the said revision was rejected affirming the order of the learned Joint District Judge. The defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) then preferred the above mentioned civil revision before the High court Division and obtained rule. A single Bench of the High Court Division ultimately, after hearing both the parties, made that rule absolute holding that the final decree was not in conformity with the preliminary decree and set aside the entire final decree and directed the trial court to draw up a fresh final decree in accordance with the preliminary decree by appointing a fresh Advocate Commissioner.

6. Being aggrieved by this judgment and order of the High Court Division the present appellants preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2062 of 2008 before this Division and this Division granted leave to consider the submissions of the learned Counsel for the leave-petitioners which has been stated in the leave granting order as quoted below:-

"Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioners submitted that in view of the fact that the defendant-respondent Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) did not prefer any appeal either against the preliminary decree or final decree passed in the suit, the High Court Division was wrong in not holding that the final decree passed in the suit cannot be set aside by invoking sections 151 or 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure inasmuch as the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) failed to point out any clerical or arithmetical mistakes in the final decree arising therein from any accidental slip or omissions on the part of the learned trial court in passing the final decree and that the learned High Court Division developed a third case that the final decree was not drawn up in accordance with the preliminary decree although the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) did not raise up any such issue in their application under sections 151 and 152 of the Code filed for correction of the final decree. The learned Counsel further submitted that in view of the fact that the learned Advocate Commissioner having failed to serve notice upon the lawyer or the representatives of the defendant Nos.1(a) to 1(d) sent notice upon them of the date of commission work by a registered postal notice dated 06.06.2005 with A/D and duly completed the commission work in presence of the parties, the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the commission work was done secretly and without knowledge of the defendant Nos.1(a) to 1(d). The learned Counsel finally submitted that in view of the fact that demolition of a part of the one storied building of the defendants is required to the extent of 1(one) decimal of land encroached by the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) in constructing their building from the share of the plaintiffs during pendency of the suit and that for effecting delivery of possession to the plaintiff-petitioners in respect of allotment of their shares in Chita dag No. 1 of the map of the final decree the demolition was necessary, the High Court Division was wrong in holding that such demolition of the defendants building to the extent of 1(one) decimal of land encroached by the defendants from the plaintiffs' share was not in conformity with the preliminary decree passed in the suit."

7. We have heard Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Senior Advocate for the plaintiff-appellants and Mr. Noor Hossain, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1.

8. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan has argued that the High Court Division has committed a serious wrong in allowing the defendants' application under sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment/ correction of the final decree and thereby setting aside the entire final decree giving direction to the trial court for drawing up a fresh final decree after appointing a new Advocate Commissioner. The learned Advocate has contended that the High Court Division did not consider at all the facts and circumstances of the case and also the legal aspects; that after passing of final decree it cannot be set aside on an application under sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that final decree was not drawn up in conformity with the preliminary decree. The learned Advocate has argued also that in this case the Advocate Commissioner effected partition quite in accordance with the preliminary decree allocating separate shaham to both the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) in accordance with the preliminary decree and the defendants did not raise any objection against this Advocate Commissioner's report or did not file any application for review of the final decree or did not prefer any appeal against that final decree. The learned Advocate has argued that at the time of effecting partition the Advocate Commissioner, on measurement, found that the defendants encroached about I decimal of land of the plaintiffs' share and as such he allocated that about I decimal land in the saham of the plaintiff to make effective partition of the property in question in accordance with the preliminary decree. The learned Advocate has contended that the High Court Division's findings that the Advocate Commissioner did not effect partition in conformity with the preliminary decree is most erroneous.

9. Mr. Noor Hossain, the learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) has made submissions to the effect that the High Court Division, on consideration of the facts, circumstances .and materials on record rightly found that the final decree was not in conformity with the preliminary decree and as such it rightly set aside the final decree. However, the learned Advocate for the respondents could not deny the fact that in the preliminary decree the plaintiffs were allotted a shaham for 3-2/3 =3.67 decimals of land and the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) were allotted a separate shaham for .06(117/120) =6.97 decimals of land out of divisible land and the Advocate Commissioner allocated shares to the respective parties for the same quantum of land.

10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and those of the trial court and the revisional court below.

11. Admittedly, the plaintiffs and the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d)-the three brothers-jointly purchased 5½ decimals of land of the suit plot from its original owners in the year 1964 and since then they had been possessing their respective shares in that purchased land amicably. The plaintiffs filed the partition suit on the allegation that the defendant Nos. 1 started construction in that purchased land encroaching some land of their share. During pendency of that partition suit the plaintiffs prayed for temporary injunction restraining the defendant No.1 from constructing any structure encroaching their share in that purchased land and the court passed an order of maintaining status quo, but in spite of that the defendants continued construction claiming that they had been making that construction on their own land. The plaintiffs then filed a miscellaneous case praying for punishment of the defendants for violating that status quo order and the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) filed written objection in that case stating that, if on disposal of partition suit the plaintiffs get their share from the lands possessed by the defendants the defendants would have no objection to give up possession of that land. In the written objection filed in violation case No. 37 of 2000 these respondent Nos. 1 (a) to 1(d) stated thus:

“বাটোয়ারা মোকাদ্দমা নিষ্পত্তি শেষে বাদীগণ যদি তাহাদের হিস্যা অনুযায়ী বিবাদীগণের সম্পত্তির অন্দরে ছাহাম পান সেই ক্ষেত্রে অত্র বিবাদীগণ দখল ছাড়িয়া দিতে আপত্তি থাকিবে না।”

12. However, from the Advocate Commissioner's report and the sketch map attached thereto it appears that both the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) were allocated separate sahams for 3-2/3 decimals and .06(117/120) decimals land respectively in accordance with the preliminary decree. The defendants 1(a)-1(d) though have made allegation that the plaintiffs were allocated saham of 3-2/3  decimals land taking some land from their possession but they did not make any allegation that they were not allocated saham for the entire land allotted to them in the preliminary decree or that they were not in possession of the land allocated to them in the final decree or that they were allocated the saham encroaching others land. So, it is obvious, that these defendants were in possession of excess land than their actual share. It also appears from the Advocate Commissioner's report and the sketch map attached thereto that it was not feasible to allocate the shares of the plaintiffs and the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) keeping the building of the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) in the saham of the defendant Nos. 1 (a) - 1(d) intact. So, the plaintiffs were allocated their saham of 3-2/3 decimals of land including some portion of the constructed building of the respondent Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) covering about 1 decimal of land which these defendants had been possessing in excess of their shares.

<u>13. We don't understand why the learned Judge of the High Court Division held that the final decree was not in conformity with the preliminary decree. The High Court Division appears to have committed further wrong in holding that the trial court gave direction to the effect that the parties will get saham maintaining their respective possession and as such the allocation of a portion of the building constructed by the defendants-in the saham of the plaintiffs was beyond the preliminary decree. In fact the trial court, in its judgment, stated thus:</u>

<u>"বাদীগণ একত্রে .০৩(২/৩) একর বাবদ একটি এবং বিবাদীগণ একত্রে .০৬(১১৭/১২০) একর সম্পত্তি বাবদ প্রত্যেকের দখল অনুসারে একটি পৃথক ছাহা, পাইতে পারে।”</u>

<u>14. This observation of the trial court does not say at all that if any of the parties is found to have been in possession of more land than his actual saham that possession also will have to be maintained. In partition suit, in awarding preliminary decree, the courts generally make order for maintaining possession of the parties in effecting partition, but that does not mean that the possession of the parties, even if in excess of their actual saham allotted in the preliminary decree, shall have to be maintained. That will be an absurd proposition. In fact the direction in the preliminary decree for maintaining possession of the parties is actually for maintaining possession as far as practicable. In effecting partition if it is found that any party is in possession of more land than his actual share then there is no bar in allocating that excess land to the share of other parties to make an effective partition of the property. Here in the present case the learned Advocate Commissioner, on measurement, found that the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) were in possession of more land than their actual share and they encroached that land from the share of the plaintiffs and constructed a building covering that encroached land. It has already been pointed out above that during pendency of the partition suit the plaintiffs prayed for temporary injunction alleging that the defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d) started construction encroaching their lands and the court issued an order for maintaining status-quo, but inspite of that the defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(d) continued construction work for which the plaintiffs filed a violation case and the defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(d) filed written objection in that violation case stating that if at the time of effecting partition it was found that they encroached any land of the plaintiffs than they would give up possession of that encroached land. However the learned Advocate Commissioner did not commit any wrong at all in allocating the excess land which was in possession of the defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(d) in excess of their actual share-in the saham of the plaintiffs.</u>

15. The High Court Division's observation that the commission work was done secretly beyond the knowledge of the defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(d) also is not well-founded. It has been categorically asserted before us that the learned Advocate Commissioner sent notices of the commission work to the learned lawyer and representative of the defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(d) by registered post with A/D and completed the commission work in presence of the parties. We find no cogent material before us to hold that the defendant Nos. 1(a)- 1(d)-who contested the suit-could not know about the measurement work done by the learned Advocate Commissioner These defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(d), admittedly, did not file any objection against this Advocate Commissioner's report. Long several moths after acceptance of this Advocate Commissioner's report and passing of the final decree they filed the application under sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for correction/amendment of final decree.

<u>16. However, we find no infirmity or impropriety in the final decree. Rather, we find this final decree quite in conformity with the preliminary decree. The High Court Division committed wrong and illegality in setting aside the final decree-entirely on an application under sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The findings and decision of the High Court Division are quite erroneous and as such these cannot sustain.</u>

17. In the circumstances this appeal succeeds.

18. Hence it is Ordered that this appeal be allowed on contest without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Amin J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment dated March 13, 2004 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1862 of 1991 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated March 6, 1991 of the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Sherpur in Other Appeal No. 77 of 1988 reversing the Judgment and decree dated July 31, 1988 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Sribordi, Sherpur in Other Class Suit No. 64 of 1985 decreeing the same.

<u>2. The suit was filed seeking declaration of title and for recovery of khan possession of the land in suit. It is the case of the plaintiffs that they have purchased the land in suit by the kabala dated January 19, 1980 from defendant No. 4, Nahar Ali, who purchased the same from Pyar Mamud, father of defendant Nos. 1-3 by the kabala dated September 19, 1974, that since purchase plaintiffs were possessing the land till they were dispossessed by the principal defendants, that defendant No.1, son of Pyar Mamud filed an application before the local Circle Officer under the provision of Ordinance No. 28 of 1976 but the same was dismissed on April 22, 1981, that defendant No.1 in collusion with the personnel of the local Revenue Officer managed to procure a forged order showing allowing the application filed by defendant No.1 and on the basis thereof dispossessed the plaintiff on April 9, 1985, that defendant No.1 did not get any order in his favour from the office of the local Revenue office on the application filed under the provision of Ordinance No. 28 of 1976 and no order for dispossessing the plaintiffs from the land in suit was issued from the office of the local Revenue Office, that by the forged and fabricated order of the Officer of the local Revenue Office brought into existence by the defendant No.1 no title and interest was created in favour of the defendant No.1 in the land in suit, that by the said forged and fabricated order defendants have not acquired any title or interest in the land in suit, that in the proceeding initiated upon the application filed by the defendant No.1 in the office of the local Revenue Officer the plaintiffs were not made parties.</u>

3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1-3 by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint. The suit was also contested by defendant Nos.5 and 7 by filing separate sets of written statement upon denying the case of the plaintiffs. The case of the defendants is that Pyar Mamud, father of the defendant Nos. 1-3 was the owner of the land in suit and during economic distress of the year 1974 he sold the land to defendant No.4, that after the death of Pyar Mamud the defendants as well as the heirs of Pyar Mamud filed a petition under the provision of Ordinance No. 28 of 1976 before the Revenue Officer and thereupon Revenue Case No. 809 (XIII) of 1976-77 was registered and the same was allowed by the order dated July 3, 1981, that in pursuant to the order of the Revenue Officer defendants paid Tk. 250/- on August 8, 1981 and obtained the receipt and on May 13, 1985 paid Tk. 250/- and obtained the receipt, that after the payment of first installment Revenue Officer passed order directing the relevant officer to hand over possession of the land in suit to the defendants and the said personnel of the Revenue Office, Sribordi made over possession to the defendants on April 11, 1982 and thereupon filed report as to delivery of possession in the office of the Revenue Officer, that plaintiffs' father impleading defendant Nos. 1, 5 and others initiated a proceeding in the Court of Magistrate on March 7, 1983 under section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but the same was rejected on September 4, 1983, that while the defendant Nos. 1-3 and other heirs of Pyar Mamud were in possession of the land the defendant No.3 sold 7½ decimals of land to defendant No.5 on October 13, 1985 and defendant Nos.1 and 2 sold 15½ Decimals of land defendant No.5 on October 12, 1985, that defendant Nos. 1-3's mother and their full sister sold 12 decimals of land to defendant No.7 on October 12, 1985, that defendant Nos. 5 and 7 on the basis of their purchase are in possession of their purchased land.

4. The trial Court considered the Ext.3, the order of the Circle Office (Revenue) dismissing the petition filed by the defendant Nos. 1-3 and others in the light of the provision of Ordinance No. 28 of 1976 and the Ext. C i.e. order of the Circle Officer (Revenue) on the basis whereof it was claimed by the defendants that their petition filed under the provision of Ordinance No. 28 of 1976 was allowed and thereupon arrived at the finding that the said Ext. C is not genuine and thereupon observed as such what ever the papers filed by the defendants in support of their assertion that they did their part what was directed by the order of the Circle Officer (Revenue) can not be accepted and merits no consideration. The trial Court also held that from the materials on record it is seen that the defendants in collusion with the personnel of the Circle Office (Revenue) has obtained the order Ext. C and as the order Ext. C is collusive, the subsequent activities of the defendants are not legal and the said activities are the product of collusion between the defendants and the personnel of the Circle Office (Revenue) and that the plaintiffs have established their case. On the aforesaid findings the trial Court decreed the suit.

5. The defendants, in all 4, went on appeal. The appellate Court on consideration of the materials on record arrived at the finding that in the absence of the record of the case which was started on the application of the defendants filed under Ordinance No. 28 of 1976 it is difficult to arrive at the finding as to which of the exhibits i.e. Exts.3 and c is genuine but as the defendants on the basis of Ext. C has gone into possession of the land in suit and as in pursuant to the Ext. C defendants have paid some of the installments and as such Ext. C carries much more weight than the Ext.3 that in case Ext. C is genuine in that case plaintiffs claim of title is not entertainable in law and as such plaintiffs are not entitled to the relief sought in the suit. On the aforesaid findings allowed the appeal and thereupon set aside the judgment and decree appealed.

<u>6. Thereupon the plaintiffs move the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction. The High Court Division in the background of the materials on record did not accept the contention of the defendants that the Circle Officer (Revenue) allowed the petition filed under Ordinance No. 28 of 1976 and thereupon considered the Ext. C as not genuine. The High Court Division on consideration of the evidence of P.W.3 held that the Ext.3 is genuine and the Ext. C is not genuine and the same has been issued by an incompetent person and the Ext. C is product of forgery, that appellate Court while making its decision as regard to the genuineness of the exts. 3 and c did not consider the evidence of P.W.3 and as such the finding of the appellate Court as to the genuineness of the Ext. C being contrary to the evidence of P.W.3 the same is not sustainable, that there is no credible evidence from the side of the defendants in support of their contention of paying installment on the basis of Ext. c, that the defendants have not filed any receipt showing payment of money on the basis of Ext. C, that defendants on the basis of fraudulent paper i.e. Ext. C entered into the land in suit upon dispossessing the plaintiffs, that since the defendants went into possession of the land in suit upon dispossessing the plaintiffs on the basis of forged and fabricated paper, their possession can not be considered to have been obtained legally or it can not be said that the defendants went into possession of the land in suit legally, that the Court of appeal below was in serious error in arriving at the finding as to the genuineness of Ext. C upon total disregard of the evidence of P.W.3 and other materials on record. On the aforesaid finding High Court Division made the Rule absolute.</u>

7. We have heard the learned Advocate-on-record and perused the materials in the paper book. It is seen from the judgment of the lower appellate Court that the said Court arrived at the finding as regard the genuineness of Ext. C upon surmise and conjecture and that in arriving at the finding as to the genuineness of Ext. C the appellate Court did not at all consider the evidence of P.W.3 who has deposed that the signature appearing in Ext.3 is of the Circle Officer, Revenue, Sribordi and that Ext. C has been issued by an unauthorised person.

8. In the afore state of the matter we do not find any reason to interfere with the judgment of the High Court Division setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate Court and thereby restoring the judgment and decree of the trial Court.

9. Accordingly the petition is dismissed.

End.
