full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Matin, J.: These two appeals are directed against the common judgment and order dated 28.01.2002 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal Nos. 108 and 203 of 1995 dismissing the appeals and affirming the judgments and decrees dated 16.02.1995 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Suit Nos. 25 and 16 of 1992 dismissing the suits.

2. The facts in short are that the appellants in C.A. No.8 of 2005 i.e. Mohiuddin Khan and another as plaintiff filed the above Title Suit No. 16 of 1992 on 06.02.1992 against the heirs of Shihamul Haque since deceased and others stating, inter-alia, that they by kabala Nos. 1586, 1588, 1589 and 1600 dated 01.02.1974, 15.02.1974, 11.02.1974 and 14.02.1974 respectively purchased .54 acres of land appertaining to C.S. Plot No. 248 of C.S. khatian No. 235 corresponding to S.A. khatian No. 406 of mouza Chandana PS. Joydebpur, District-Gazipur described in schedule 'A' of the plaint from Chaturi Tanti and got delivery of possession and by Mutation Case No. 170/74-75 their names were mutated in S.A. Khatian No. 406 in place of said Chaturi Tanti and they paid ground rents and got dakhilas. Against the above order of mutation, Shihamul Haque preferred Misc. Appeal Case No. 13 of 1981 claiming title on the basis of deed of exchange (settlement) dated 16.06.1980 and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka, by order dated 12.01.1982, without at all giving any finding as to possession of the suit land cancelled the mutation. The appellants then filed Appeal No. 8 of 1982 and the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka who heard the appeal, heaving found that the appellants and others were in possession of the case land, set aside the above order dated 12.01.1982 and restored the mutation in the name of appellants and others. Then Shihamul Haque preferred Appeal No. 96 of 1984 before the Board of Land Administration and after hearing the same was dismissed. Shihamul Haque then filed Writ Petition No. 159 of 1989 and the High Court Division, after hearing declared that the above orders passed by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka and the Board of Land Administration are without any lawful authority with the observation that the question of title and ownership and validity of the deeds in question could be gone into and decided only by a civil court. The appellants out of the proceedings of the above Misc. Appeal Case No. 13 of 1981 and also from the contents of the annexures of the above Writ Petition No. 159 of 1989 for the first time came to know about the alleged deed of agreement for exchange dated 30.10.1963, the alleged powers of attorneys dated 07.06.1965, the deed of exchange dated 16.06.1980 in terms of Exchange Case No. 35/69-70, Title Suit Nos. 27 of 1971 and 150 of 1972, Civil Revision Nos. 315 and 1387 of 1977 and also of the withdrawals of the same on 29.01.1980 and 21.01.1980 which were referred in the above proceeding. The appellants are bonafide purchasers of the suit land for valuable consideration without any notice of agreement of exchange and other facts as stated above. Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 (E. P. Disturbed Persons Rehabilitation Ordinance, 1964) having died by the efflux of time on 31.12.1964 as held in 17 DLR 451, the above proceeding of Exchange Case No. 35/69-70 stated on 24.07.1969 for forfeiting the land of the appellants for the purpose of granting so-called settlement is without jurisdiction. The possession of the property in question was always with the appellants and was never taken over by Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka or Sub-Divisional Officer and the same was never enlisted in the Census List of 1966-1967.

3. The contesting defendant Nos. 1(a) to 1(d), the heirs of Shihamul Haque contested the above suit by tiling written statement denying the claim of the appellants and stating, inter-alia, that Shihamul Haque, his father Enamul Haq and his mother Tahera Sogra Begum, were the inhabitants of Bardwan District in India and after they settled in the then East Pakistan in 1950 migrating from India, Chaturi Tanti along with Shibulal, Bhutu, Surjagaya and Nathuri Tanti proposed to exchange their lands including suit land of the above mouza Chandana with the land of Shamsul Hoque, Enamul Hoque and Tahera Sogra Begum at Bardwan and then a deed of agreement was duly executed which was registered on 30.10.1963 and pursuant to the above agreement the parties handed over the possession of their respective lands to each other acknowledging delivery of possession. Embargo being created upon, the Hindus to transfer their properties by registered deed of conveyances on promulgation of defence of Pakistan Rules several powers of attorney were given to each other by both sides on the basis of which exchange deeds were executed in Bardawan in India and by one of such deed of exchanged dated 09.08.1968 executed in India Tahera Sogra Begum exchanged 1.36 acres of her lands at Bardwan with .89 acres land of Chaturi and Nathuni Tanti of mouza Chandana which includes the suit land. Bhatu Tanti, Chaturi Tanti and 3 others made joint declaration before the Notary Public in Calcutta on 15.07.1968 and 12.08.1968 confirming the above exchange of their lands of mouza Chandana including the suit land. The facts of the execution and registration of the above agreement to exchange in the year 1963, the irrevocable power of attorney and the exchange deeds were duly certified by the Magistrate, First Class, Alipur, West Bengal, India on 17.07.1968 and 10.09.1968. Shihamul Haque applied to the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka praying for permission to execute and register the deed of exchange under the authority of general power of attorney executed in his favour whereupon the above Exchange Case No. 35/69-70 was started. Shibulal Tanti, Chaturi Tanti and others filed an objection in the above exchange case contending, inter alia, they did not enter into any such agreement nor did they exchange their properties and that the exchange deed is fraudulent and powers of attorney are collusive and were vitiated by coercion, threat and intimidation. Shibulal Tanti also filed Title Suit No. 27 of 1971 in the 1st Court of Sub-Judge, Dhaka against Shihamul Haque and others challenging the deed of agreement for exchange, powers of attorney as well as the deed of exchange but the suit was dismissed for non-prosecution and-subsequently he prayed for restoration of the suit which was rejected by order dated 08.06.1972 and thereafter Shibulal Tanti filed Title Suit No. 150 of 1972 in the same court against Shihamul Haque and others seeking same declarations as made in the previous suit and then prayed for amendment which was rejected as the suit filed earlier was dismissed. Against this order of rejection Tanti filed Civil Revision No. 315 of 1977 and also filed Civil Revision No. 1372 of 1977 on more or less similar grounds. Then both the above Rules were discharged on the basis of prayers of Tanti to the effect that they do not want to press the Rules, after the disposal of the above suits/revisions Shihamul Haque applied to Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka to proceed with the above Exchange Case No. 35 of 1969-70 who then after making necessary, enquiry and after completing all the formalities executed and registered the deed of exchange (Settlement) on 16.06.1980 transferring 7.12 acres of land of mouza Chandana in favour of Shihamul Haque thereafter on the basis of the above deed of exchange Shihamul Haque started Mutation Appeal Case No. 13 of 1981 in the office of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka, praying for canceling the earlier mutation in the name of the appellant and got the mutation cancelled. The subsequent order as stated earlier were passed by the Additional Divisional Commissioner, Dhaka in Appeal Case No. 8 of 1982, the Board of Land Administration in Appeal No. 86 of 1984 and the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 159 of 1980 made the Rule absolute with the observation that the question of title and validity of the deed of exchange could be decided only by the civil court. The defendants have been possessing the suit land along with other lands by cultivating and growing crops therein through bargadars namely Kamal's mother and her son-in-law.

4. The appellants in C.A. No. 9 of 2005 i.e Sree Monmohan Shaha and another as plaintiff on 25.02.1992 filed the above Title Suit No. 25 of 1992 against the heirs of Shihamul Haque and others claiming similar reliefs on more or less similar averments made in the above Title Suit No. 16 of 1992, variation being that the area of the suit land was .98 acres as described in schedule A, B and C of the plaint, the appellant No. 1 purchased from Shibulal Multi 0.02 acres of land of Plot No. 1952 of Khatian No.68, 0.35 acres of land of Plot No. 1905 of Khatian No. 290, .05 acres of land of Plot No.1916 of Khatian No.429 i.e. total .06 acres, all within the said mouza Chandana by registered kabalas dated 24.01.1979 and appellant No. 2 also purchased .06 acres of land of the aforesaid Plot No. 1916 and some other land from aforesaid Plot No.1952 by registered kabala dated 06.01.1979 from the aforesaid Shibulal Tanti and they were put into possession of the suit land immediately. They had filed the Separation and Mutation Case No. 1384 of 1978-79 in the office of C.0.(Rev.), Joydehpur and their names were mutated in S.A. Khatian Nos.68, 290 and 429 under the order of C.O.(Rev.) dated 19.06.1979 and they have been paying ground rent for the suit land since 06.09.1979. The plaint of the above suit also contained averments regarding filing of Misc. Appeal Case No.13 of 1981 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka, Appeal No. of 1982 before Additional Commissioner, Appeal No. 96 of 1984 before Board of Land Administration and Writ Petition No. 159 of 1989 before the High Court Division and in the above suit the defendant Nos. 1(a)-1(d), the heirs of Shihamul Haque also filed written statement making averments similar to in their written statement filed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1992.

5. The trial court by judgment and decree dated 16.02.1995 dismissed both Title Suit Nos. 16 and 25 of 1992. The appellants preferred First Appeal Nos. 108 and 203 of 1995 and the High Court Division after hearing dismissed both the appeals holding, inter-alia, that Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka was competent and legally authorized to execute and register the deed of exchange (settlement) and it is not necessary that the property should be declared either as enemy property or vested property for its vesting upon the government for regularizing the pending genuine exchange cases including the instant one. The plaintiff-appellants having not filed the suits with in three years from the date of knowledge of the settlement deed as required under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, the suits are hopelessly barred by limitation. The plaintiff-appellants, during the pendency of the suits/civil revisions which were admittedly filed by their vendors made the purchases without the permission of the court and so the above purchases of the plaintiffs are hit by the principles of lis pendens as provided under Section 52 of the Transfer of property Act. The plaintiff-appellants having not paid proper court fees as required for the several reliefs as sought, the suits are also hit by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and Section 7 of the Court Fees Act. After withdrawal of the suit or dismissal of a suit for non-prosecution for default no fresh suit can be filed by the same parties or any party claiming through them on the same subject of dispute without the permission of the court and as the earlier suits including the civil revisions being dismissed for non-prosecution, the present suits being filed without obtaining permissions, are not maintainable.

6. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants in Civil Petition No. 1759 of 2002 submitted that the appellant having prayed for declaration of title of the disputed land which became clouded in view of the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 02.12.1991 passed in Writ Petition No. 159 of 1989 setting aside the order of mutation in favour of the appellants, the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the suit filed by the appellants in  the year 1992 was barred by limitation. The appellants not being party to the deed of exchange (settlement) dated 16.06.1980 it was not necessary for them to seek declaration that the said deed is invalid and the appellants having purchased the disputed land in 1974 as bonafide purchasers for value without notice the deed of settlement cannot affect the title of the appellants. No issue was joined by the parties as regards the enemy status of the disputed property and the High Court Division, having found the disputed property not being an enemy property, erred in law in holding that the Government under Act XLV of 1974 acquired the authority to execute the deed of settlement. The High Court Division upon an erroneous view of the provisions of Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act wrongly held that the purchase of the appellants was barred by the principles of lis pendens. The High Court Division was wrong is not noticing that the instant suit is on a different cause of action arising out of order dated 02.12.1991 of the High Court Division clouding the title of the appellant. The suits filed by the original owners of the disputed cause of action arising from the creation of documents relating to exchange of the disputed property and so the provisions of Order 23 Rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding withdrawal/dismissal are not applicable and the High Court Division was wrong in not properly considering the evidence of both the parties on the question of possession of the disputed land.

7. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellants in Civil Petition No. 1758 of 2002, adopted the above submissions.

8. Leave was granted to consider the have any affect on the plaintiff's title above submissions in both cases.

9. Heard Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Counsel appearing for the appellants in C.A. No. 8 of 2005 and Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel appearing for the appellants in C. A. No. 9 of 2005 and Mr. T. K. Khan and Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-4 in both cases and perused the petition and the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other papers on record.

10. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel submits that the appellants having prayed for declaration of title to the disputed land which became clouded by the judgment of the High Court Division passed on 02.12.1991 in the writ petition setting aside the order of mutation in favour of the appellants, the High Court Division was wrong in holding the suit filed by the appellants in 1992 to be barred by limitation.

11. Mr. T. H. Khan, the learned Counsel on the other hand submitted that the plaintiff appellants had the knowledge of the settlement and therefore the courts below were right in holding that the suit is barred by limitation because the suits were not filed within 3 years from the date of knowledge of settlement.

12. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel submits that the appellants were not a party to the deed of settlement and therefore it was not necessary for the appellants to have a declaration of invalidity of the said documents and when the plaintiff purchased the land in 1974 a deed of settlement long after i.e. in 1980 cannot have any affect on the plaintiff's title.

13. He further submits that the settlement being void ambition as the Government had no title on the land need not be avoided by the plaintiff and therefore the question of limitation did not arise.

14. It appears that the cause of action of the suit arose on 02.12.1991 when the High Court Division set aside the mutation of the appellants in respect of the suit land and the suits were filed in 1992 and therefore the suits were well within time.

15. The learned Counsel submits that the suit land was never enemy property or vested property and never vested in the Government and therefore the settlement of a land by the Government which did not belong to the Government is void ignition and it need not be avoided by filing a suit and therefore the plaintiff were not obliged to challenge the settlement dated 16.06.1980 as they purchased the land in question from the original owner by registered sale deeds in 1974.

16. In such view of the matter the courts below erred in law in holding that the suits are barred by law.

17. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the Counsel appearing for the appellants submits that the High Court Division found that the disputed land is not enemy property and the P.W.1 admitted in his deposition that it is not enemy property or forfeited property and therefore the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the Government acquired the suit land under Act XLV of 1974 and had the authority to grant the settlement.

18. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel submits that in the case of Chitta Ranjan Sutar Vs. Secretary, Judicial Department reported in 17 DLR 451 both Sections.4 and 6 of the Ordinance No.1 of 1964 were declared ultravires and Ordinance No.I of 1964 became a dead law in 1964 and this position was reiterated in the case of Abdul Majid Bepari Vs. Kashem Ali Maloo reported in 27 DLR 1 and therefore the GOs issued under a dead law namely Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 were ineffectual and moreover the alleged forfeiture was not done under Ordinance No. I of 1964.

19. It appears that Sections 4, 6 and 6A of the Ordinance No.I of 1964 were declared ultravires the Constitution and therefore the position is as if Sections 4, 6 and 6A of the Ordinance No.I of 1964 had never been passed at all.

20. Mr. Willoughby was quoted in the case of 27 DLR to explain the position of an unconstitutional law which runs as under:-

"An unconstitutional act is not a law, it confers no right, it imposes no duties, if offers no protection, it creates no office; it is in legal contemplation, as inoperative as though it had never been passed."

21. It appears that the deed of settlement Annexure-J in the paper book was issued under the authority of Act XLV of 1974 and not under Ordinance No. 1 of 1964. Moreover D.W.1 in her deposition categorically admitted “বিনিময় মোঃ ৩৫/৬৯-৭০ তে ২০/১১/৭০ইং তারিখে জেলা প্রশাসক এর দেয়া নোটিশে উল্লেখিত, সম্পত্তি বাজেয়াপ্তকৃত সম্পত্তি নয়।”

22. Thus it appears that the Government had no authority to forfeit the land under Section 6A of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and in fact it did not forfeit under Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 and there is nothing on record that the property was enemy property or vested property and therefore the Government had no authority to grant settlement of the land in question in favour of the defendants and the High Court Division was wrong in holding otherwise.

23. The High Court Division found that the suits are hit by doctrine of Iis pendens and also under Order 23 Rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

24. Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act runs as under:-

"52. During the (pendency) in any Court (in Bangladesh) of (any) suit or proceeding (which is not collusive and) in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question, the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be therein, except under the authority of the Court and on such terms as it may impose."

25. It appears that the suits filed by the original owners in 1971 were on different cause of action and cause of action of the present suits are all together different. The earlier suits were for declaration that the deed of agreement for exchange, powers of attorney as well as the said exchange deed effected in West Bengal are illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff in that Suit No. 27 of 1971 and Suit No. 150 of 1972 was filed praying for the same reliefs as were prayed in Title Suit No. 27 of 1971. But the present suits are for declaration of title and possession and a further decree for declaration that the settlement deed in favour of the defendant is void and not binding upon the plaintiff. Therefore the cause of action of the present suits being all together different the principle of Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act as quoted above has no manner of application inasmuch as in the earlier suits right to immovable property was not directly and specifically in question whereas in the present suits right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question.

26. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel has referred to the case of Shanmughasundaram Pillai Vs. Parvathi Ammal and another reported in AIR 1945 Madras 454 where it was held that for the doctrine of lis pendens to apply, the right to specific immovable property must be directly in issue.

27. Order 23 Rule 1(3) runs as under:-

"Where the plaintiff withdraws from a suit; or abandons part of a claim, without the permission referred to in sub-rule (2), he shall be liable for such costs as the Court may award and shall be precluded from instituting any fresh suit in respect of such subject-matter or such part of the claim."

28. As we have already held that the subject matter of the present suits and the earlier suits are not same and therefore Order 23 Rule 1(3) has no manner of application in the present case.

29. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that the suit on a different cause of action even though related to the same property is not barred.

30. In support of his contention the learned Counsel has referred to the case of the Order of the Holy Cross Vs. Lonnappan Thattil and another reported in AIR 1990 Kerala 215.

31. Mr. Mahmudul Islam has also referred to the case of Amir Hossain Khairati being dead his heirs: Altaf Hossain and others Vs. Abdul Aziz Beoari and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 106 and submitted that since the suits were dismissed for non-prosecution Order 23 Rule 1(3) has no manner of application. In that case, this court held as under:-

"From the averments made in the plaint it appears that Title Suit No. 7 of 1983 was dismissed for non-prosecution and that suit was not withdrawn by the plaintiffs. As such, the provision of Order 23 Rule 1(3) is not applicable as the order of non-prosecution of the earlier suit does not amount to withdrawal. Hence the plaintiff is not precluded to file a fresh suit by making out a new cause of action on fresh averments made in the subsequent suit."

32. Therefore the finding of the High Court Division that the suits are barred under Order 23 Rule 1(3) is also not tenable in law.

33. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that both the courts below failed to appreciate the evidence on record on the question of possession of the suit land. He has taken us through the deposition of P.Ws. and D.Ws. and particularly P.W.2 who was nephew of Chaturi the vendor of the plaintiff who supported the plaintiffs possession.

34. He also referred to evidence of P.W.3 who testified that the plaintiff constructed houses on the suit land.

35. Mr. Islam has referred also to the deposition of D.W.2 who admitted in his cross-examination that he did know the suit land.

36. He also referred to the deposition of D.W.4 who also admitted that he did not know the suit land and submitted that the finding of the High Court Division on possession is contrary to the evidence on record.

37. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Counsel adopted the argument of Mr. Mahmudul Islam on other points but on the question of possession he referred to written statement of the respondents submitted in the suit in para-45 where the respondents admitted that they were dispossessed by the appellants from the homestead land and exchange lands during pendency of the exchange case.

38. In para-55 in the written statement the respondents admitted that they were dispossessed in August 1972.

39. Mr. Bhuiyan has taken us to the evidence of P. W. s and D.Ws. and also referred to P.W.1 who testified that having purchased the suit land he is possessing the same by constructing houses thereon. In his cross-examination the plaintiff asserted that when he purchased the suit land from his vendors no suit was pending.

40. He has also referred to the evidence of P.W.3 who asserted that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land having houses thereon and cultivable lands.

41. He has also referred to the evidence of P.W.5 who asserted the plaintiffs possession with houses thereon and D.Ws.2 and 3 who admitted that they did not know the suit land.

42. We have perused the evidence ourselves and found that the plaintiffs sufficiently proved their possession in the suit land and the defendants are admittedly out of possession and therefore the finding of the High Court Division and the trial court on this point arc not tenable in law.

43. Mr. T. H. Khan, the learned counsel appearing for the respondents on the other hand submitted that they entered into an agreement for exchange as early as on 30.10.1963 with the vendors of the appellants, obtained power of attorney in 1965, but ultimately the land was forfeited in favour of the Government as per provision of Section 6A of the East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964 and the Government as the owner of the land granted the deed of settlement for 7.12 acres of land. The respondents handed over their lands in favour of the vendors of the appellants but because of the legal bar could not get the exchange deeds registered and therefore the courts below rightly dismissed the suits.

44. He has referred to Ordinance No.I of 1964 and submitted that as per explanation to Section 4 of the Ordinance the word 'transfer' shall include ----- the exchange and any agreement for such exchange and since the transfer was done in violation of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 as per Section 6A of the Ordinance the land stood forfeited to the then Government.

45. Mr. Khan has also referred to 43 DLR (AD) 137 and submitted that the GOs referred to in the judgment on the basis of which settlement has been give in favour of the respondents by the Government are all valid GOs having force of law.

46. It appears from the judgment in the case of Chitta Ranjan Sutar that both Sections 4.6 and 6A were declared ultravires the Constitution and therefore the position is that Sections 4.6 and 6A never existed before. Moreover the Ordinance No.I of 1964 died a natural death by a efflux of time and the exchange proceeding case No. 35 of 1969-70 having been started on 24.07.1969 to forfeit the land and for settlement has been done without any lawful authority.

<u>47. Moreover the property in question was never enlisted in the census list of 1966-67 and admittedly the land in question was not forfeited land as per the position of D.W.1 and the deed of settlement in question refers to Act XLV of 1974 and it does refer to Ordinance No. 1 of 1964. The case referred to by Mr. T. H. Khan reported in 43 DLR (AD) 137 relates to vested property and has no manner of application in this case.</u>

<u>48. In view of our discussions as above it appears that the plaintiffs proved their case and they were entitled to a decree as prayed for and the findings of the courts below on the maintainability of the suits are not tenable in law.</u>

49. Mr. T. H. Khan, the learned Counsel submits that the plaintiff of both the suits are merely claiming part of the land covered by the deed of settlement and therefore they are not entitled to decree as prayed for.

50. Be that as it may since the judgments of the courts below suffers from gross illegality these are liable to be set aside and the plaintiffs are entitled to a decree in respect of the title to the suit land and a further coerce that the deed of settlement. Annexure-J to the paper book, on the basis of Exchange Case No. 35 of 1969-70 is not binding upon the appellants of both the suits.

51. In the result both the appeals are allowed and the impugned judgment and decree are set aside.

52. Both the suits are decreed. In Title Suit No. 16 of 1992 the plaintiffs do get a decree declaring that the plaintiffs had right, title, interest and possession in the suit land described in schedule 'A' of the plaint and a decree -for declaration that the settlement deed described in schedule 'B' is not binding on the plaintiffs.

53. Title Suit No. 25 of 1992 be decreed declaring that the plaintiffs have right, title, interest and possession in the suit land described in schedule 'A', 'B' and 'C' of the plaint and a decree for declaration that the settlement deed described in schedule 'B' is not binding on the plaintiffs.

End.

full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana, J. <u>This Civil Appeal, by leave, at the instance of Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate represented by Chairman, Court of Wards and Chairman, Land Reforms Board and Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate represented by Manager, Land Reforms Board has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 05.04.2003 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 229 of 2001 rejecting the prayer for withdrawal of the suit and also dismissing the appeal. These appellants, as plaintiffs, instituted Title Suit No. 15 of 1999 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka for declaration of title in the suit property stating, inter-alia, that the suit property originally belonged to Nawab Sir Salimullah which devolved upon the Court of Wards under the Court of Wards Act, 1879 and the land was recorded in the C.S. Khatian and also S.A. Khatian in the name of Court of Wards on behalf of Nawab Sir Salimullah. That the property cannot be given in settlement by anybody other than Board of Revenue of the Court of Wards, but the defendants claimed title over the suit property on the' basis of alleged settlements allegedly granted in their favour by the chief Manager of Court of Wards, that the alleged settlements of the suit land in favour of the defendants are fraudulent, collusive and illegal and that these alleged settlements created cloud in the title of the plaintiffs and hence the plaintiffs felt constrained to institute the suit.</u>

<u>2. The defendant Nos. 9 to 18 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter-alia, that the suit was not maintainable, that the Chief Manager of the Court of Wards settled the suit property in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 before the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force and after getting settlement the defendant Nos. 1 to. 8 were enjoying the suit properties on payment of revenue and taxes and the suit properties also were recorded in their names. That these defendants along with 29 others purchased the suit land from the settlement holders by 32 different registered kabalas and the khatians also were prepared in their names and they paid rents and have been possessing the suit property. That in an earlier snit being Title Suit No. 386 of 1989 this present plaintiff No. 1 filed written statement admitting that the manager of the Court of Wards though did not possess the power to settle the lands situated in Dhaka City, but he had the power to do so for the lands situated outside Dhaka City. That the settlements of the suit property by the manager of the Court of Wards in favour of the vendors of the contesting defendants were valid in law.</u>

3. Both the parties examined one witness only each in order to prove their respective cases and produced some papers which were marked exhibits The trial court, on consideration of these oral as well as documentary evidence, dismissed the Suit by the judgment and decree dated 27.11.2000.

<u>4. Being aggrieved by this judgment and decree of the trial court the plaintiffs preferred First Appeal No. 229 of 2001 before the High Court Division. In the midst of hearing, of the appeal the plaintiff-appellants filed an application under order 23 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh stating, inter-alia, that at the time of filing of the suit there were some formal defects for which the suit might fail.</u>

<u>5. The High Court Division, after hearing the learned Counsel of both the parties, rejected the said application for withdrawal of the suit for the reason only that it was filed at a belated stage and also dismissed that first appeal on merit by the impugned judgment and order.</u>

6. Leave to appeal against this judgment and order of the High Court Division was granted by this Division to consider the submission of the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-leave-petitioners that the High Court Division committed error in rejecting the application for withdrawal of the suit on the ground only that the application was a belated one.

7. We have heard the learned Counsel of both the sides.

<u>8. Mr. A. F. Hasan Ariff, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants has made submissions to the effect that order XXIII rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure has authorized the court to grant permission to the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with the liberty to sue afresh at any time after its institution on the ground of formal defects and also on other sufficient grounds and that by virtue of section 107 of the same Code of Civil Procedure the appellate court also possesses this power of granting permission to the plaintiff-appellants to withdraw from the suit; that in the present case the plaintiff-appellants filed an application before the appellate court for withdrawal of the suit stating clearly that there were some formal defects for which the suit might fail, but the appellate court, without considering at all the grounds stated in that application for withdrawal of the suit, rejected the same on the ground only that the said application was filed at a belated stage. Mr. Hasan Ariff has argued that where the law permits withdrawal of the suit at any time after its institution and where it is now settled by so many decisions of the apex courts that a suit can be withdrawn at the appellate stage also, the High Court Division was not justified at all in rejecting the application for withdrawal of the suit on the ground only that it was filed at a belated stage. The learned Counsel has argued that the High Court Division ought to have considered the ground for withdrawal of the suit mentioned in that application. The learned Counsel has contended that had the High Court Division considered the grounds for withdrawal of the suit it would not have rejected the application on the plea only that it was filed at a belated stage. The learned Counsel has stated also about the formal defects of the suit. He has stated that some other persons also require to be added as defendants in this suit and prayer for some consequential reliefs, such as confirmation of possession and permanent injunction against the defendants also need to be added in this suit. The learned Counsel has submitted that the High Court Division has committed error in rejecting the prayer for withdrawal of the suit without considering at all these formal defects in framing the suit and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set aside. In support of his submission the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants has cited the cases of Mohammed Abdul Quddus Vs. Mohammad Mustafa Hussain, reported in 12 BLD(AD) 131, Madan Mohon Vs. Abdus Samad, reported in 32 DLR at page 176 and Dil Mohammad Vs. Jamir Hossain, reported in 58 DLR at page 88. In all these cases permission for withdrawal of the suit was granted at the appellate stage on the ground of formal defect and also on other sufficient grounds.</u>

<u>9. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Counsel for the defendant-respondents though has made some submissions supporting the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, but ultimately he did not strongly oppose the prayer of the plaintiff-appellants for withdrawal of the suit. The learned Counsel, however, has pointed out that for institution of a fresh suit the plaintiff-appellants shall be bound by the law of limitation in the same manner as if this present suit had not been instituted. Drawing our attention to rule 2 of order XXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure the learned Counsel has submitted that since in this suit it was rather an admitted fact the plaintiff-appellants were out of possession at the time of filing of the suit, the fresh suit, if filed, will be barred by limitation.</u>

<u>10. In reply to this submission of the learned Counsel for the defendant-respondents Mr. A. F. Hasan Ariff, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants has strongly argued to the effect that nowhere either in the plaint or in deposition of the witness the plaintiff ever admitted that they were not in possession of the suit land, that the contesting defendants also, by adducing evidence, could not prove at all that the plaintiffs were out of possession or the defendants were in possession of the suit land. Mr. Hasan Ariff has also drawn our notice to the application for withdrawal of the suit and stated that in this application also it was not stated that the plaintiffs were out of possession. The learned Counsel has stated also that in the leave granting order only this court erroneously mentioned that in the application for withdrawal of the suit it was stated that the plaintiffs being out of possession there was defect in the suit. The learned Counsel has contended that it was an error made by the court and that for this erroneous statement made by the court it cannot be said at all that the plaintiff-appellants were out possession of the suit land. Mr. Hasan Ariff has argued also that on examination of all the materials on record it will be very much evident that nowhere in the plaint, nor in the evidence, nor in the application for withdrawal of the suit there is any admission at all to the effect that the plaintiffs are out of possession of the suit land and that the contesting defendants also did not try even to prove by adducing necessary evidence that the plaintiffs are out of possession or they (defendants) are in possession of the suit land.</u>

11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Counsel of both the sides and gone through the impugned judgment, that of the trial court, the evidence adduced by both the parties and other materials on record.

12. It appears that in this suit both the contesting parties examined only one witness each in order to prove their respective cases. From the side of the plaintiff Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate, one Assistant Manager of Court of Wards, Land Reforms Board was examined as P.W. 1. This witness has deposed to the effect that Court of Wards did not settle the suit land in favour of anybody and that in S.A. Khatian No. 3 the suit land has been recorded in the name of Court of Wards. This witness has produced also a photocopy of a certified copy of S.A. Khatian No. 3-(which the court marked as exhibit-3) showing that the suit land has been recorded in the name of Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards state. The P.W. 1 has specifically denied also the defence case that the Chief Manager of the Court of Wards settled the suit land in favour of the defendants and that the defendants were possessing the suit land. During cross-examination this witness of the plaintiffs has further specifically denied the defence suggestion that the plaintiffs were not possessing the suit land. It also appears that to this P.W. 1 a suggestion was put from the side of the defendants to the effect that the S.A. and R.S. Khatians of the suit land were collusive and that after getting summons of this suit the defendants could know about these S.A. and R.S. Khatians of the suit lands. This defence suggestion, rather, supports the plaintiffs' case that 'the suit land has been recorded in the S.A. and R.S. Khatians in the name of the plaintiff.

13. D.W. 1, the only witness from the side of the contesting defendant, though deposed to the effect that the suit land was settled in their favour, but it appears that none of these alleged settlements of the suit land in favour of the defendants have been proved at all. This D.W. 1 though produced some alleged certified copies of some alleged filed 'parchas' of the suit land but it appears that none of these alleged field 'parchas' has been proved to be genuine. Where the defendants admitted that the suit land was recorded in the name of the Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate in both 'S.A. and R.S. Khatians by giving specific suggestion to the D.W. 1 to the effect that both those khatians were collusive-the alleged field 'parchas' of the suit land should have been taken into consideration cautiously. But it appears that no attempt was mate either from the side of the defendants or from the side of the court to be sure that those alleged field 'parchas' produced by the D.W. 1 were genuine though from the side of the plaintiffs it was specifically alleged by giving suggestion to the D.W. 1 that those field 'parchas' were collusive. However, it appears that this D.W. 1, during cross-examination, has stated that he was defendant No. 16, and was deposing on his behalf only and that the other defendants did not give him any power to depose of their behalf also. To this D.W. 1 specific suggestion was given from the side of the plaintiffs that the defendants did not possess the suit land.

14. In this suit it is an admitted fact that the suit land belonged to the plaintiff Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate and the plaintiff was also in possession of the suit land. In these circumstances, in this suit, the onus is heavily upon the contesting defendants to prove their alleged case that they took Settlement of the suit land from the Chief Manager of the plaintiff Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate and they got possession of the same and are also in possession of the same. But it appears that except the D.W. 1-one of the contesting defendants himself-no other witness has been examined before the court either to prove the alleged settlement of the suit land in favour of the defendants or to prove the defendants' possession in the suit land. In these circumstances how the courts below could say that the plaintiffs had no title and possession in the suit land and also that the defendants are in possession of the suit land. It appears that the High Court Division did not at all examine the evidence on record, rather made some statements in the impugned judgment to the effect that the trial court considered the evidence adduced by the contesting defendants and found title in favour of the defendants. The High Court Division itself, in spite of being the appellate court, did not examine the evidence adduced by the parties and did not consider at all whether the findings and decisions of the trial court was justified and correct without examining the evidence on record and without forming any opinion of its own as to the truth, genuineness, acceptability etc. of the evidence adduced by the parties the High Court Division dismissed the appeal simply making comment to the effect that since the plaintiff could not prove their possession in the suit land and since the defendants had been found in possession the suit has been rightly dismissed. We don't understand how the High Court Division could say that the defendants have been found in possession of the suit land where the trial court also did not find possession of the defendants in the suit land. It appears that the High Court Division in its impugned judgment stated also that the only witness of the plaintiffs did not assert that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. But on scrutiny of the evidence of P.W. 1 we find that thin. P.W. 1 has categorically denied the defence suggestion that the plaintiffs are not in possession of the suit land. We have already pointed out before that where, admittedly, the plaintiff Dhaka Nawab Court of Wards Estate was the owner in possession of the suit land the onus is heavily upon the defendants to prove that they are now in possession of the suit land. But the defendants have failed to discharge that onus.

<u>15. Mr. Hasan Aniff, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants has stated also that this plaintiff No. 1 did not file any written statement in Title Suit No. 386 of 1989 stating that the Chief Manager of the Court of Wards had authority to settle the land situated outside Dhaka City. This statement of Mr. Hasan Ariff has not been controverted by the learned Counsel of the defendant-respondents. Rather this statement of the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellants gets support from exhibit- 'Cha'</u>

<u>16. However, considering all these facts and circumstances we find that the High Court Division did not do justice in rejecting the plaintiff-appellants application for withdrawal of the suit on the ground of formal defects for the reason only that it was a belated application. The impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, therefore, need to be set aside.</u>

17. In the result this appeal succeeds.

18. Hence it is ordered that the appeal be allowed on contest without any order as to cost.

19. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division and that of the trial court are set aside.

20. The plaintiff-appellants are permitted to withdraw from the suit with liberty to sue afresh.

End.

full_judgment:
Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman J: Instant application under Article 103 of the Constitution is for granting leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 31.10.2007 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division making the Rule absolute issued in Civil Revision No.3906 of 1997.

<u>2. The Civil Revision was filed challenging the judgment and decree dated 29.09.1997 passed in Title Appeal No.07 of 1994 by the Additional District Judge and Ante-Smuggling Tribunal, Sylhet, allowing the appeal reversing the judgment and decree dated 30.11.1993 passed in Title Suit No.54 of 1993 by the Court of Assistant Judge, Bishwanath, Sylhet, decreeing the suit granting permanent injunction.</u>

3. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 hereof, are the plaintiffs in Title Suit No.54 of 1993 filed in the Court of Assistant Judge, Bishwanath, Sylhet, against the defendants, who are the petitioner and Respondent No.3 of the leave petition. The suit, was for a decree for permanent injunction restraining the said defendants from interfering with the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs of the suit land.

<u>4. The facts relevant are that the plaintiffs' father Nosibullah was the admitted owner of the suit land and said Nosibullah died leaving behind one son (plaintiff No.1), one daughter (plaintiff No.2) and a grandson (defendant No.2) by his predeceased-daughter Korfulennessa. After the death of Korfulennessa, the defendant No.2 was brought up by the grand father at his residence and after the death of Nosibullah said defendant No.2 stayed for sometime in the said home and thereafter the said defendant No.2 along with his father left the house giving up his right, title and interest in the suit land and started living at village Sridharpur, about 5 miles away from the suit land, and thus the plaintiffs have been exclusively possessing the suit land, as owners and possessors, and enjoying usufructs therefrom paying rents and taxes regularly to the Government. The defendant No.2 subsequently sold a portion of land to defendant No.1, a Londoner, by a registered sale deed and taking advantage of such registered sale deed, the defendant No.1 started threatening to forcible entry into the suit land. Hence the suit.</u>

5. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement claiming ownership and possession in the suit land by way of inheritance by defendant No.2 and affirming the sale of land by defendant No.2 in favour of the defendant No.1 through registered sale deed dated 17.03.1993, alleging, amongst others, that the name of mother of defendant No.2 Korfulennessa being a co-sharer, through whom he inherited, appears in the record of right along with the names of the plaintiffs and that through an amicable partition said defendant No.2 Abdul Bashir got the suit land exclusively in his saham and he sold the suit land to the defendant No.1 within the knowledge of the plaintiffs and delivered possession thereof and that the suit has been filed malafide and liable to be dismissed.

6. The learned Assistant Judge framed 5 issues namely: -

1. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

2. Do the plaintiffs have cause of action to file the suit?

3. Do the plaintiffs have exclusive possession over the suit land?

4. Do the plaintiffs have prima-facie right, title and interest on the suit land?

5. Are the plaintiffs entitled to get decree as prayed for?

7. The plaintiffs examined three witnesses and the contesting defendants also examined three witnesses.

8. The trial Court on consideration of the oral and documentary evidences on record and the submissions of the learned' Advocates of the contesting parties, has found that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land. The learned Court observed that the defendant No.2 although claimed about an amicable partition but no document or evidence could be produced before the Court in support of said claim.

<u>9. The learned Court on scrutiny of the depositions of the D.Ws. held that the defendants failed to prove the claim of their possession on the suit land. The D.W. 2, himself admitted that. defendant No.2, Abdul Bashir was never in possession of the suit land. D.W. 1 who deposed, as an attorney of defendant No.1, stated that he was not present at the time of alleged taking over of the possession of the suit land by the defendant No. 1. Thus the Assistant Judge disbelieved the story of possession of the defendant in the suit land as claimed. However having regard to acquiring of right and title in the suitland through inheritance and the fact of leaving the grand father's residence by the defendant No.2 for permanently residing at a place 5 milies away therefrom, the learned Court found presumptive possession in favour of the plaintiffs. Thus the Assistant Judge decreed the suit. Being aggrieved there against the defendants filed Title Appeal No.7 of 1994 in the Court of District Judge, Sylhet, which on transfer was heard and disposed of by the Additional District Judge and Anti-smuggling Tribunal, Sylhet, on contest. The appellate court below on consideration of the issues framed by the trial Court and the answers given as to the maintainability, cause of action, prima-facie right, title and interest of the plaintiffs, disbelieved the claim of exclusive possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land and allowed the appeal and thereby dismissed the suit observing, amongst others, that the D.Ws have proved the sale deed dated 17.03.1993 and also delivery of possession, since the defendant No.2 being in possession of the suit land delivered the possession to defendant No. 1.</u>

10. The appellate Court on consideration of the deposition of the plaintiffs' witnesses disbelieved the possession of the plaintiffs observing that the witnesses could not state the plot and khatian numbers and that the defendant No.2 being an admitted co-sharer by inheritance in the suit land, has sold the land in favour of the defendant No.1 by registered sale deed dated 17.03.1993 and thereby the defendant No.2, and for that matter after the purchase, the defendant No.1 is in possession of the suit land and therefore no permanent injunction can be allowed. Therefore, the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court was set aside. Being aggrieved there-against plaintiffs as petitioners moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3906 of 1997, the Rule issued therein was heard and disposed of by a Single Bench of the High Court Division vide judgment and order dated 31.10.2007 making the Rule absolute and setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court below and restored the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Bishwanath, Sylhet, in Title Suit No.54 of 1993, allowing the permanent injunction.

<u>11. The High Court Division in disposing of the Rule observed that both the plaintiffs and defendant No.1 inherited the suit property from the admitted owner Nosibullah and that defendant No.2 inherited share in the suit land and that he left the residence of his grand-father and became a permanent resident of a place 5 miles away therefrom and there being no partition of the suit land, the High Court Division believed the presumptive possession of the plaintiffs on the suit land and discarded the findings of the appellate court below as to possession of the defendants observing that:</u>

<u>"Learned Additional District Judge held that none of 3 P.Ws could mention khatian and plot number of the suit land while they were cross-examined by the learned defence counsel. But this finding has no merit at all since it is admitted that the plaintiffs had title thereto. Learned Additional District Judge placed reliance upon the evidence of 3 defence witness. D.W.1 Anowar Hossain was the Attorney of defendant No.1 Azam Khan, purchaser of the suit land from the defendant No.2 he was the brother-in-law of defendant No. 1. The said D.W. 1 could not also state the boundary and plot number of the suit land when cross examined by the learned advocate for the plaintiffs. D.W.2 Mosoddor was also related to D.W. 1 Anowar Hossain and defendant No.1 Azam Khan. He stated that he was the paternal uncle of Azam Khan (defendant No.1)</u>

<u>He also stated in his cross-examination that he could not state the boundary and plot number of the suit land. If the learned Additional District Judge disbelieved plaintiffs possession in the suit land only because of the said 3 P.Ws having failed to state in their cross-examination the plot and khatian number of the suit land, fail to understand how he believed in defendant No. 1's possession in the suit land when D.W.1 and D.W.2 failed to Mention the boundary and plot number of the suit land. Moreover D.W.1 Anwor Hossain and D.W.2 Masaddar Khan were also closely related with defendant No. 1. D.W.3 was the scribe of the kabala whereby defendant No.2 transferred the suit land in favour of the defendant No.1. He was not a witness of possession.</u>

<u>Under the aforesaid circumstances discussed by me above. I have reason to hold that the learned Assistant Judge rightly held that the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land in its entirety could be treated to be their presumptive possession, the defendants having failed to prove any partition taking place amicably or by mets and bounds placing defendant No.2 in exclusive possession thereof. The learned Additional District Judge could not reverse the said finding of the learned Assistant Judge by showing any cogent ground or reason. His findings appear to be quite faulty on the face of the evidence and materials on record which I have elaborately discussed in this judgment."</u>

12. The High Court Division in-length discussed the depositions of the witnesses as well as the exhibits and found that the defendant No.2 is also a co-sharer in the suit land and he has sold the suit land in favour of the defendant No. l by registered kabala on 17.03.1993 but possession could not be given as the possession was with the plaintiffs and that there was no partition of the suit land.

<u>13. We have perused the leave petition and the judgment of the High Court Division as well as those of the courts below. Admittedly the suit property belonged to Nosibullah and after his death the said land was inherited by the plaintiff Nos. l and 2, being son and daughter, and by defendant No. 2, being son of the predeceased daughter Korfulennessa, and that as per law of inheritance in the plaintiff Nos. 1 and 2 and defendant No.2 are co-sharers to the extent of their respective shares and that plaintiffs were in physical possession of the suit land and that the suit land not being partitioned the said plaintiff Nos.1 and 2 and defendant No.2 were in ejmali possession, though the defendant No.2 was not in physical possession, and that the defendant No.2 being a co-sharer has sold out his share to the defendant No.1 in the suit land, thereby the defendant No.1, subject to validity of his purchase, became a co-sharer in the suit land and he may pursue his claim for possession through a partition suit, if so advised. We have also perused the deposition of the P.Ws and D.Ws, copy annexed to the leave petition, and observe that the P.Ws. stated about possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land but could not state the plot numbers whereas the D.W.2 in his cross-examination has stated that “আব্দুল বসির ৩ বৎসর পূর্বে শ্রীধরপুর চলিয়া যায়। নালিশী বাড়ী হইতে সোয়া মাইল দূরে হইবে।” which goes to show that the defendants could not have any possession on the suit land. The D.W.1 claimed about the possession of the defendant No.1 on the suit land through bargadar but no bargadar was adduced to corroborate the fact of possession of the defendant No.1 and said D.W.1 stated that the village Sridharpur, where the defendant No.2 resides, was about six mile away from the suit land. The D.W.3 was the scribe of the sale deed. He only proved the sale deed and payment of the consideration money. D.Ws.1 and 2 also could not state the plot and khatian numbers of the suit land.</u>

14. Thus we are of the view that the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division suffers from no illegality and calls for no interference.

15. Accordingly, the application for leave to appeal is dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana, J. <u>This Civil Appeal, by leave, at the instance of Bangladesh represented. By the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and others, is directed against the judgment and order dated 18.09.2014 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1337 of 2014 making the rule absolute. Bangladesh Private Medical College Association (respondent herein) filed the above mentioned writ petition challenging the increase of the minimum "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 out of total 200 marks for admission to M.B.B.S. course for the session 2013-2014 communicated by memo No. Sha: ODhi/Chi: Shi:/Borti/MBBS/2013-2014/204 dated 05.11.2013 issued by the respondent No. 4 (Annexure-A-1 to the writ petition). The case of the writ petitioner, in short, is that the writ-petitioner association is comprised of members representing private medical colleges of Bangladesh. The primary responsibilities of the writ-petitioner is to ensure, amongst others, that all the private medical colleges maintain an enhanced standard of education for their students, which will enable them to acquire all the necessary academic and practical medical experiences before obtaining the M.B.B.S. decree. That the respondents No. 1 (Secretary Ministry of Health and Family Welfare) framed a guidelines for admission of students in M.B.B.S/B.D.S. courses (the Nitimala, 2011) stipulating qualification criteria for admission of students in the B.B.B.S/B.D.S. courses in all Medical/Dental Colleges (public/private) in Bangladesh. Clause 22 of that Nitimala, 2011 states, inter-alia, that an application must acquire a combined grade point average (G.P.A.) of minimum 8.00 in his/her respective S.S.C. and H.S.C. examinations from the Science Faculty provided he/she does not carry less than G.P.A. 3.50 in any of the aforesaid examinations. The respondent No. 1 by an office order being No. ShaKomo/Chishi-1/Be: Me: Co: cha: Borti-01/2011/843 dated 04.12.2012 stipulated, amongst others, the admission criteria for the M.B.B.S/B.D.S. courses for the session 2012-2013 according to which an applicant is required to have merit score of 110 for being eligible to get admission to the M.B.B.S. course. That to the Knowledge of the writ-petitioner the aforesaid office order dated 04.12.2012 was not amended, neither the respondent No. 1 nor the respondent No. 2 (Director General, Directorate of Health Services) informed the writ-petitioner or its members of any such change. That in the notice dated 27.08.2013 issued by the respondent No. 2 inviting applicant for admission to M.B.B.S. course for the session 2013-2014 there was no mention that the applicants should have minimum merit score of 120 for being eligible for admission. But the respondent No. 1 in its meeting dated 23.09.2013 recommended that in order to be eligible for admission an applicant must have a minimum "cut-off" marks of 120 out of total marks of 200 for his/her admission to M.B.B.S. course for the session 2013-2014 and thus introduced a new minimum qualification criteria for admission raising the "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120. The writ Petitioner has stated that considerable number of seat in private medical/dental colleges for the session 2013-2014 are still vacant after the admission of students to the M.B.B.S. course due to this increase of minimum "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120. That the writ-petitioner submitted an application dated 2.01.2014 before the respondent No. 2 to consider the admission criteria of B.B.B.S. course as well as, to extend the deadline of the admission, pursuant to which the respondent No. 2 by memo being No. Sha: ODhi:/Chi: Shi:/Bibidho Bishoy. 2012/31 dated 07.01.2014 recommended that the minimum merit score for an applicant to be eligible for admission in M.B.B.S. course should be fixed at 105 instead for 120. The writ-petitioner submits that if the private medical/dental colleges are not allowed to admit students on the basis of the memo dated 04.12.2012 the concerned private medical colleges will suffer irreparable losses and injuries since 30% to 40% of the total seats in each private medical colleges would remain vacant. That the potential candidates also are approaching the writ-petitioner for redress of this situation.</u>

2. Rule was issued in the above writ petition. None of the respondents appeared before court to oppose that rule. A Division Bench of the High Court Division, after hearing the learned Counsel for the writ-petitioner, made that rule absolute by the impugned judgment and order making observations to the effect that the advertisement inviting applications for admission to M.B.B.S. and B.D.S. courses for the session 2013-2014 there was no mention about any "cut-off" mark, rather it was only mentioned that the candidates would require to have at least GPA 8.00 in total in both S.S.C. and H.S.C. examinations with condition not to have less than 3.5 GPA in any of the said examinations and that in the guidelines dated 21.07.2011 (annexure-C) to the writ petition) also there is no stipulation about the said "cut-off" mark and that by circular dated 04.12.2012 the respondents set the "cut-off" mark at 110 and pursuant to that circular dated 04.12.2012 advertisement for admission test was published on 31.08.2013 and that the new "cut-off" mark of 120 has been introduced subsequently pursuant to the meeting dated 23.09.2013 with back dated effect, affecting the rights of the writ-petitioner and the students aspirant for admission to M.B.B.S. an B.D.S. courses. The High Court Division noticed also that by a sub-sequent letter dated 07.01/2014 the respondent No. 4 informed all concerned that the "cut-off" mark for admission to M.B.B.S. and B.D.S. courses for the academic session 2013-2014 would be 105 and extended also the dated of admission till 31.01.2014. The High Court Division directed the respondents to allow the private medical colleges to admit students for the academic session 2013-2014 with a "cut-off" mark 105.

3. Leave to appeal against the judgment and order of the High Court Division was granted to consider the submissions of the learned Attorney General to the effect that the decision raising the "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 for admission to the M.B.B.S. course was taken by the appropriate authority in compliance with the Nitimala of 2011 and that this decision is a policy decision of the concerned authority and as such it cannot be challenged before court and that there has been no illegality and no violation of natural justice also in taking this decision and that this decision has not violated the fundamental rights also of the members of the writ-petitioner association in any way.

4. At the time of hearing of this appeal also the learned Attorney General has made the same submissions. The learned Attorney General has argued before us also to the effect that the impugned decision raising the "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 for admission to the M.B.B.S/B.D.S. courses is a policy decision of the authority concerned and that considering the prevailing circumstances and to ensure quality education for the M.B.B.S./B.D.S. students the authority concerned has rightly increased this "cut-off" mark and there has not been any illegality at all in taking this decision. The learned attorney General though has frankly conceded the fact that this decision raising the "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 for admission to M.B.B.S./B.D.S. course has not been taken by Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (BMDC) constituted as per section 4 of Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council Act, 2010 has argued that the impugned decision of raising the "cut-off" mark has been taken by the concerned authorities many of whom are members of BMDC and that this decision has been taken as per 'Nitimala' of 2011 which was approved by the BMDC and has contended that in the circumstances this decision cannot be said coram non-judice. The learned Attorney General has made submissions to the effect also that the impugned decision of raising the "cut-off" mark for admission to M.B.B.S/B.D.S. courses was taken with a view to improve the quality of education of the students of M.B.B.S/B.D.S. courses and it has not violated the fundamental rights of the members of the writ-petitioner in any way and in the circumstances the High Court Division has committed wrong in making the rule absolute.

<u>5. Mr. M. Amirul Islam, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the writ-petitioner-respondent has made submissions to the effect that the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council Act, 2010 is an Act of parliament and it came into force in the year 2010 and that according to this law Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council has been formed and this council (BMDC) is empowered to decide the guidelines and other criteria for admission to the M.B.B.S/B.D.S. courses; that the impugned decision increasing the "cut-off" mark for admission to M.B.B.S./B.D.S. courses being admittedly, not taken by this Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council is coram non-judice and as such illegal The, learned Counsel has alleged also that this increase of "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 was taken whimsically and arbitrarily after the admission test was over and as such it has prejudiced both the writ-petitioner association as well as the students seeking admission to M.B.B.S/B.D.S. courses. Refuting the argument of the learned Attorney General, Mr. M. Amirul Islam has submitted also that the committee which took the impugned decision of raising the minimum "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 cannot be said in any way a substitute for Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (BMDC) and as such this committee was not authorized at all to take this decision which was absolutely within the domain of BMDC and as such this impugned decision being coram non-judice is illegal. The learned Counsel for the writ-petitioner-respondent has made submission to the effect also that many of the private medical colleges have already admitted some students with the "cut-off" mark which was set by the respondents for the previous session of 2012-2013 and in the circumstances these students and also the private medical colleges will have to suffer much if the impugned decision raising the "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 is not declared illegal. The learned Counsel has drawn our notice to Annexure-L to the writ petition which shows that 23 private medical colleges have admitted total 224 students who scored less than 120 marks and has submitted that these 224 students may be allowed to continue their study in the M.B.B.S. course, otherwise they will be seriously affected.</u>

<u>6. We have considered the submissions of the learned counsel of both the sides and the facts and circumstances and the materials on record. Admittedly, the impugned decision raising the minimum "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 was taken by a committee headed by the respondent No. 1 and not by the Council, namely, Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council (BMDC) which has been formed as per law, namely, Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council Act, 2010. Section 5 of this Act shows that this Council (BMDC), is empowered to deal with almost all the matters relating to Medical and Dental Institutions including framing of guidelines etc. for admission to M.B.B.S. and B.D.S. courses. The setting of "cut-off" mark for being eligible for admission to M.B.B.S. an B.D.S. courses falls within these powers of BMDC and as such the BMDC only is empowered to fix or set the minimum "cut-off" mark for being eligible for admission to these courses. Admittedly, the impugned decision raising the "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 was not taken by this BMDC, rather it was taken by the respondent No. 1 and some other persons It might be that some of the members of the committee which took this decision of raising the "cut-off" mark were members of this BMDC also, but that did not authorize that committee to assume the power of BMDC. So, it is apparent that the impugned decision raising the "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 being not taken by the BMDC was coram non-judice and as such illegal.</u>

7. From the submissions of the learned Counsel of both the sides and the materials on record it appears that some of the private medical colleges have already admitted some students to M.B.B.S. course who could not score the minimum "cut-off" mark set by the impugned decision. As we have found this impugned decision raising the "cut-off" mark from 110 to 120 illegal the students who have already been admitted to different private medical colleges should be allowed to continue their study.

<u>8. We, therefore, hold that total 224 students, who have already been admitted to 23 different private medical colleges, as has been stated in annexure-L to the writ-petition, are entitled to continue their study in the respective medical colleges where they got admission.</u>

9. This Civil appeal thus be dismissed with the above observations. This judgment will govern the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 1110 of 2015 and 1111 of 2015 also.

End.
