case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 15.03.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4806 of 2004)
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain, J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 15.03.2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 4809 of 2009 discharging the Rule and affirming the judgment and decree dated 31.10.2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, In-charge, Sixth Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 551 of 2003 allowing the appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 23.07.2000 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Third Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 54 of 1994 dismissing the suit. The facts, leading to the filing of this petition, in brief, are:

2. The petitioner herein as the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 54 of 1998 in the Third Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Dhaka against defendant Nos. 2-9 for recovery of khas possession in respect of .3920 ajutangsha, of land in Mouza-Kamrangirchor, Old Khatian No. 45, Hal Khatian No. 67, Old Plot No. 158 and new Plot No. 208, described in the schedule to the plaint. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that Fazar Ali, Misir Ali, Omar Jan and Jamela Bibi were the owners of the suit land and that by amicable partition, the suit land along with other lands fell in the saham of Misir Ali. After that, Misir Ali died leaving daughter, Fulbanu as his only heir. While Fulbanu had been owning and possessing her inherited; land, the recorded owners made a partition by a registered deed being No. 2378 dated 05.05.1964 and Fulbanu got .95 acre of land in her saham. After that, Fulbanu gifted .47 1/2 acre of land of plot No. 158 and .11 1/2 acre of land of plot No. 208 to his son, the plaintiff Md. Sorboddi Miah by a registered deed of gift dated 27.10.1977 and delivered possession thereof to him and S.A. record was correctly prepared in the name of his vendor. After that, the plaintiff mutated his name and paid rents and while in need of money, the plaintiff transferred part of his land to different purchasers except the suit land and the purchasers mutated their names and have been paying 'rents regularly. The defendants declared in the locality that they have right and title in the suit land which had created cloud over the title of the plaintiff and in such circumstances, he filed Title Suit No 153 of 1990 in the then Second Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the defendants. Meanwhile, the defendants failed to take any step in that suit and therefore, the Court decreed the suit on 23.01.1992 declaring right and title of the plaintiff in the suit land Against the said decree, the defendants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 15 of 1992 'which was dismissed and after that, the defendants filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 241 of 1995 which was also dismissed for default on 06.10.1996. Having been: defeated in the suit, the defendants along with some hired miscreants dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land on 22.11.1997 Hence, the suit land has been filed by the plaintiff for recovery of possession.

3. Defendant No. 1 contested the 'suit by filing written objection denying all the material statements made in the plaint. His case, in short, is that the plaintiff with the help of some miscreants abducted his father Falu Miah with a view to killing him to grab the suit land and since then, he has been missing. The plaintiff has no right, title and possession in the suit land, which 'never fell in the saham of Fulbanu on the basis of partition deed dated 05.05.1964 The plaintiff did not get any possession in the suit land on the basis of alleged deed of heba dated 27.10.1977 executed and registered by his mother Fulbanu The suit brought by this plaintiff is false and is liable to be dismissed.

4. Defendant Nos. 6, 9-10 contested the suit by filing written objection denying all the material statements made in the plaint Their case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to Sheikh Akbor, who died leaving two sons, namely, Fazar Ali and Misir Ali, one daughter, 'Omarjan and a widow Jamela Bibi. After that, Misir Ali died leaving' behind his mother, brother and sister and a daughter Fulbanu. After death of Jamela Bibi, her son, Fazar Ali and daughter Ornarjan inherited 33/40th share of the suit khatian and they amicably partitioned the ejmali land by a registered deed of partition dated 24.03.1939 and the land of suit plot Nos. 158 and 204 had entirely fallen in the saham of Fazar Ali. Thereafter, Fazar Ali died leaving behind wife, Gulbodon and two minor daughters and Gulbodon on her behalf and on behalf of her minor daughters transferred the suit land to Barkutullah Munshi by a: registered deed of sale dated, 13.09.1950. Barkatullah in his turn sold the same to Abdul All by a registered deed of sale dated 11.04.1951. Abdul Ali married Fulbanu, daughter of Misir Ali and defendant No. 1, Falan @ Falu Mia was born out of their wed-lock. Falu Mia (defendant No. 1), transferred 'the land of suit plots to defendant No. 2. by a registered deed, of sale dated 28.07.1979, to defendant Nos. 3 and 4 by a registered deed of sale dated 07.04.1979, to defendant No. 5 by a registered deed of sale dated 22.03.1979 and to the defendant-petitioners by a registered deed of sale dated 23.01.1980 The defendants were inducted into possession of the suit land and they got 'their names mutated in the khatian and have been in possession thereof. The plaintiff obtained ex parte decree in Title' Suit No. 153 of 1990 by practicing fraud and suppressing the summons of the suit. The plaintiff kidnapped defendant No. 1 on 06.12.1994 and' his son lodged a G. D. Entry being No 919 dated 22.01.1995 with Lalbagh Police Station to that effect. The plaintiff filed Miscellaneous, Case No. 15 of 1992 and Miscellaneous Appeal. No. 24,1 of 1995 by false personation in the names of defendants and those cases were dismissed for default at the instance of the plaintiff. The whereabouts of defendant No. 1 was not known to 'these defendants for about 5/6' 'years and his heirs could not be substituted in his place as the Court refused to declare his civil death. The suit is false and the same is liable to be dismissed.

5. The trial Court by its judgment and order dated 17.07.2000 dismissed the suit.

6. Against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court, the plaintiff preferred Title appeal, No. 551 of 2000 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka On transfer, the appeal was heard and disposed of by the then learned Additional District, Judge E -Sixth Court, Dhaka, who by his judgment and order dated 31.10.2004 allowed the appeal reversing the judgment' and decree of the trial Court.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment 'and decree passed by the appellate Court, defendant Nos. 9 and 10 filed a provisional application before the High Court Division and obtained. Rule in Civil Revision No. 4806 of 2004. The High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 15.03.2009 discharged the Rule without any order as to costs.

8. Feeling aggrieved, by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the leave petitioner has preferred this civil petition for leave to appeal before this Division.

9. Mrs. Madhumalati Chowdhury Barua, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing on behalf of the leave petitioner, submits that Fulbanu got the entire suit land in plot Nos. 158 and 204 by a registered deed of partition dated. 05.05.1994 and that she transferred 59 acre of land in favour of the plaintiff by a registered deed of gift dated 27.10.1977 (exhibit-4) and that the appellate Court also found that the plaintiff acquired 59 acre of land by exhibit-4 and that the High Court Division without reversing this findings of the appellate Court made the Rule absolute concurring with the findings and decision arrived at by the trial Court and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside She further submits that the appellate Court came to a finding that Title Suit No. 153 of 1990 of the Second Court, Of the then Subordinate Judge against defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 was decreed ex parte on 23.01.1992 and the defendant of that suit, thereafter, filed Miscellaneous Case No. 15 of 1992 for setting aside the ex parte decree which was dismissed and the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 241 of 1995 filed by defendant No. 1 was also dismissed for default on 06.01.1996 and that the High Court, Division without altering this finding made the Rule absolute and as such, the impugned judgment should be set aside.

10. Mr. Syed Mahbubur Rahman, learned Advocate-on-Record, appearing on behalf of respondent Nos. 1 and 2, on the other hand, supports the impugned judgment delivered by the High Court Division.

11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates-on-Record, perused the impugned judgment and the materials on record.

<u>12. The High Court Division came to a finding that by amicable partition in 1939, the suit land had fallen in the saham of Fazar Ali as evidenced by Annexure-Ka, the partition deed dated 24.03.1939, and that there was no reason to devolve the suit land on Fulbanu by the deed of partition dated 05.05.1964 The High Court Division noticed that the petition deed dated 24.03.1939 Annexure-Ka showed that Fazar Ali was the first party of that deed of partition and 1.40 acres of land of suit plot No. 158 and .23 acre of land of plot No. 204 fell in the saham of first party.</u>

<u>13. The High Court Division came to a finding that whereabouts of defendant No. 1 Fallan alias Falu Mia was not known from 06.12.1994 and that the written statement filed on behalf of defendant No 1 by his son and attorney Shahjahan was not accepted and that the latter stated that his father had been missing since 1994 and that all the RWs. stated that Fallan Mia was not traceable. The High Court Division further held that the appellate Court dismissed the suit on the finding that the plaintiff acquired title in the suit land on the basis of the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No 53 of 1990 although the defendants purchased the suit property in 1979 and 1980 and that the decree was passed in Title Suit No. 153 of 1990 without impleading the defendants and as such, the decree passed in Title Suit No 153 of 1990 was not binding on the defendants The High Court Division also held that there was no specific boundary of the suit land to identify from which portion of plot Nos. 158 and 208, the plaintiff was dispossessed and from when he was dispossessed and that in a suit for khas possession and permanent injunction without any specific boundary of the suit land, the plaintiff could not get any decree.</u>

14. The aforesaid findings of the High Court Division are based on proper appreciation of law and fact.

<u>15. The sheet anchor of the plaintiffs case is the ex parte decree obtained by him against defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 in Title Suit No 153 of 1990 Defendant No. 1 was Falan alias Falu Mia Admittedly, defendant No 1 sold the suit land to the other defendants of the present suit and those defendants purchased the suit land in 1979 and 1980 and the decree was passed in Title Suit No. 153 of 1990 without impleading those defendants and as such, those defendants, of the present suit are not at all bound by the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No 153 of 1990. It also appears that the suit land is vague and indefinite without any specific boundary and therefore, the plaintiff cannot get a decree in respect of any unspecified land and on this score alone the suit could be dismissed.</u>

In the light of the findings made before, we do not find any substance in this civil petition for leave to appeal. Accordingly, this civil petition is dismissed.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 27th day of May, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1084 of 2001)
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J. This appeal, by leave, is from the judgment and order dated the 27th day of May. 2008 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1084 of 2001 making the Rule absolute

2. Facts necessary for disposal of this appeal are that respondent Nos. 1-7 as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No.11 of 1993 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, 1 Dhaka for permanent injunction.

3. The case of the plaintiffs, in short, was that the suit plots belonged to the predecessor of the plaintiffs and the defendants and on amicable partition, the plaintiffs' predecessor got 1/3rd  share therefrom as described in schedule- 'Ga' to the plaint (hereinafter referred to as the suit land). After the death of their predecessor, the plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land. On 25.12.1992, the defendants threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession from the suit land; hence they filed the suit.

4. The defendants contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that there was no amicable partition of the suit plots in between the predecessors of the plaintiffs and the defendants and the suit plots remained in ejmali, so the plaintiffs suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable and the same was liable to be dismissed.

5. The trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 28.06.1993 dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the plaintiffs filed Title Appeal No. 242 of 1993 before the District Judge, Dhaka. The learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka on hearing the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 22.10.2000 dismissed the appeal.

6. Against the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the plaintiffs filed Civil Revision No. 1084 of 2001 before the High Court Division and a learned Judge of the Single Bench by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute, set aside the judgments and decrees of Courts below and decreed the suit. Against the judgment and order of the High Court Division, the defendants filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1741 of 2008 before this Court and leave was granted to consider the submissions of the learned Advocate for the defendant-appellants as under:

"The learned Counsel submits that the trial Court as well the appellate Court held that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land as such the High Court Division erred in law in setting aside the concurrent finding of fact by re-appreciation of the evidence which is not allowed in revisional jurisdiction. He further submits that the revisional Court can only interfere in revisional jurisdiction as well as defined exceptional jurisdiction that is misreading of the evidence and non-considering of the material evidence but which evidence is misread or which evidence is non-considered is totally absent in the judgment of the High Court Division. He lastly submits that in a suit for injunction, the plaintiffs must prove their exclusive possession. The trial Court as well as the appellate Court concurrently held that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession. The revisional Court erred in law in holding that the defendants witnesses did not deny the partition as well as the possession of the suit land"

7. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, for the appellants has made submissions in the light of the leave granting order and in support of his submissions, he has placed the evidence on record.

8. Mr. Mamtazuddin Fakir, learned Advocate, for the plaintiff-respondents, on the other hand, has supported the impugned judgment and order. He has submitted that the High Court Division rightly interfered with the judgment and decree of the Courts below and decreed the suit on consideration of the evidence on record, as both the Courts below misread the evidence on record as well as failed to consider the material evidence and as such, no interference is called for with the impugned judgment and order and the appeal be dismissed.

<u>9. From the judgment and decree of the trial Court, it appears that it dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land though it found their prima facie title in the suit land. The trial Court found the plaintiffs' ejmali possession in the suit land. The main reason of the trial Court in not finding plaintiffs' exclusive possession in the suit land was that they could not prove their case of amicable partition of the suit plots amongst their predecessors. The trial Court further observed that there was no written batwara between the predecessors of the plaintiffs and the defendants. The trial Court also observed that though the plaintiffs stated that they were in exclusive possession of the suit land through amicable partition or gharoa bantannama, they did not say in the plaint where, in what circumstances and in which year and on what date such gharoa bantannama took place; no witness was also examined in that respect. It appears to us that in coming to the said finding and giving the said observations, the trial Court misread the evidence of the PWs in respect of the plaintiffs' case of exclusive possession of the suit land on the basis of gharoa bantanama.</u>

10. PWs 3 and 4 specifically stated about the gharoa bantannama between the predecessors of the plaintiffs and the defendants and about the possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land on such gharoa bantannama. It further appears that the trial Court considered the testimony of PW 1 (plaintiff No. 3 Was examined as PW1 ) in his cross examination only and found fault with his testimony on the ground that he could not say the total area of the land though he asserted that they were in possession of the half of the suit plot being No.185. The trial Court disbelieved PWs 2 and 3 on the ground that they could not tell the chauhaddi of suit plot No.214 though both of them specifically stated about the possession of the plaintiffs therein. The trial Court on consideration of the evidence of the DWs (2DWs were examined, DW No.1 being defendant No. 1) came to the finding that from the evidence of the DWs, no proof was found how much land of the suit land the defendants possess and how they possess (in the judgment, in Bangla, it has been written as "বিবাদীপক্ষের স্বাক্ষীদের বক্তব্য হইতে ও নালিশী সম্পত্তি কতটুকু কিভাবে বিবাদীপক্ষ দখল করেন ইহার কোন প্রমাণ পাওয়া যায় না।") However, the trial Court noted that DWI in his examination-in-chief stated that the plaintiffs possess 1/3rd  of the suit land and they possess 2/3rd thereof and DW2 also stated that the defendants possess the major portion of the suit land and the plaintiffs possess less portion thereof, In coming to the facium of exclusive possession, the trial Court did not at all consider the S.A. khatians prepared in the name of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land and the payment of rents by them for the same. The Appellate Court in spite of being the last Court of fact, did not consider the evidence at all either documentary or oral; it simply dittoed the finding of the trial Court in a slip shod manner.

<u>11. From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the High Court Division made the Rule absolute on the finding:</u>

<u>"In the present case, it appears that the witnesses of the plaintiffs as well as that of defendants clearly deposed that there was an amicable partition 22/25 years back and the plaintiffs and defendants are possessing the land according to their shares, and without considering the evidence of the witnesses of both the parties, the Courts below took an erroneous view that there was no partition and as such the plaintiffs were not in possession of the suit land, It appears from the record that the plaintiffs mutated their names in the record of right and by virtue of that, they paid rents by exhibit-5 series and mutation in S.A. Khatian No. 31/7, 31/8 show their exclusive title and possession. In the present case the defendants' witnesses did not deny the partition as well as possession of the plaintiffs on the suit land. Although the trial Court found a primafacie case in favour of the plaintiffs, which, was mentioned in its judgment, dismissed the suit. The Court of appeal below affirmed it in a slip shod manner. The rent receipts, exhibit-5 series, though not document of title, are important items of evidence of possession and may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title. Central point for consideration of the Court in a suit for permanent injunction is the question of possession, which requires to be decided mainly on oral evidence adduced by the contending parties and documentary evidence usually plays a secondary role. The trial Court ignored the evidence of the witnesses examined by the contending parties while passing the judgment and the Court of appeal below committed the same mistake by failing to discuss and consider the material evidence adduced by the contending parties. The witnesses of both the parties categorically deposed that there was a partition and the parties were possessing the land as per their shares,"</u>

12. The plaintiffs prayed for a decree for permanent injunction in respect of the suit land measuring an area of 2.46 acres land in 6(six) plots being Nos. 180, 214, 185, 130, 235 and 258 as described in schedule 'Ga' to the plaint. Area of the land in each of the plots has been specifically identified by chauhaddis. Before the trial Court, the attested certified copies of the SA. khatians were filed, but were not marked as exhibits. However, Mr. Bhuiyan could not dispute the correctness of the attested copies of the khatians, The khatians show that the names of the plaintiffs were recorded separately in respect of the suit land, The vital document proved and exhibited were the rent receipts, exhibit-5 series. These exhibits show that the plain-tiffs have been paying rents in respect of the suit land, In each of the rent receipt of exhihit-5 series, all the suit plots have been mentioned and the area mentioned is 2.46, i.e. the suit land. These facts clearly substantiate the ease of the plaintiffs that there was an amicable partition amongst the co-sharers and the suit land fell in the saham of the plaintiffs and they have been in possession thereof Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan found it difficult to dislodge the legal impact of S.A. Khatian and the payment of rents separately by the plaintiffs in respect of the suit land visa-vis the oral evidence of the PWs as was found by the High Court Division.

<u>13. In the case of Moharram Ali and another-Vs-Mohammad Madhu Mia and others 41DLR(AD)92, this Division upheld the view taken by the Courts below that a co-sharer, who has been in exclusive possession of a specific and separate share of the ejmali property well demarcated by boundaries, is entitled to retain his possession  till legal partition by an order of injunction against another co-sharer who threatens him with dispossession. In that case, a learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division took a contrary view holding that since the parties were co-sharers in respect of the suit land, one co-sharer could not be prevented by injunction from claiming and exercising his right over any part of the property. From the finding of the High Court Division, it is apparent that the plaintiffs have been in exclusive possession of the suit land which is specific and well demarcated. The High Court Division rightly decreed the suit, In the context, we restate the law that even if there was not a partition, an injunction can be granted at the instance of a co-sharer in exclusive possession of a specific and separate share well demarcated by boundaries, against another co-sharer, who threatens the former with dispossession. If one co-sharer is in possession of specific part of a joint land, the other co-sharers cannot dispossess him without a suit for partition.</u>

14. Leave was granted to consider the sub-mission made on behalf of the appellants that the High Court Division erred in law in setting aside the concurrent finding of fact that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land by "re-appreciation of the evidence which is not permissible in revisional jurisdiction." But from the discussions made hereinbefore, it is clear that the Appellate Court did not at all discuss the evidence on record and it, in a slip shod manner, just affirmed the decision of the trial Court, so the findings of the Courts below cannot be said to be concurrent in its true legal' sense and therefore, to be immuned from interference by the High Court Division.

15. The trial Court also misread the evidence of the PWs as well as the DWs on the question of amicable partition in coming to the finding that the plaintiffs failed to prove their exclusive possession in the suit land, The trial Court did not also consider the S.A. Khatians recorded in the name of the plaintiffs and the rent receipts, exhibit-'5' series in that respect. Therefore, we do not see any wrong with the High Court Division in considering the evidence on record and give its finding on the question of exclusive possession of the suit land, particularly, in view of the fact that both the Courts below failed to consider the S.A. khatians and the rent receipts. Since the entire record was before the High Court Division, it had every right to go through the record and see whether the Courts below were correct in dismissing the suit on the ground that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land, From the findings of the High Court Division, it appears to us that it, in fact, considered the evidence, both oral and documentary, which the Courts failed to consider as well as misread. The instant case was a clear case of misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence by the Courts below. Therefore, it cannot be said that the High Court Division "re-appreciated" the evidence or in other words, re-assessed the evidence.

16. We have gone through the evidence on record, both oral and documentary and we find that the High Court Division rightly took into consideration the evidence on record in coming to the finding that the plaintiffs proved their exclusive possession in the suit land.

17. In view of the above, we find no substance in the appeal.

18. Accordingly, this appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, Advocate with Mrs. Rubaiyet Hossain, Advocate ----- For the petitioners. 
Mr. Probir Neogi, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Rabia Khatun and another. ------ Plaintiff-Respondent-petitioners
Vs
Amrita Lal Das being dead his heirs, Chandan Kumar Das and others ----- Defendant-Appellant Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Soumendra Sarker, J:- The Rule issued calling upon the opposite party no. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 24.11.2001 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, .Kishoreganj in Other Class Appeal No. 142 of 1994 dismissing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 27.02.1994 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Katiadi, Kishoreganj in Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 decreeing the suit, should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit arid proper. 
2. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in a nutshell, can be stated thus, the present petitioners namely Rabeya Khatun and Samsuddin filed Other Class Suit nos. (69/93(361/83)  )/(12/84(39/87) ) against one Mafiz Uddin, Amrita Lal and Government of Bangladesh for declaration of title and confirmation of possession. The .opposite party Amrita Lal Das being plaintiff filed Other Suit No. (68/93)/(499/85), against Samsuddin and his wife Rabeya Khatun for declaration of title, recovery of possession and setting-aside the judgment and decree dated 03.03.1982 passed in Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 and cancellation of a instrument executed pursuant to said decree and for declaration that the sale deed dated 27.02.1971 is void, made by false personification and without consideration. 

3. Both the suits were heard together and disposed of by the trial court in a single judgment passed on 27.02.1994 whereby Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 was dismissed and Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 was decreed on contest. 

4. The case of the plaintiff of Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 in short, is thus that the plaintiff acquired the land in dispute by way of inheritance and while he was in possession the defendants dispossessed him in the night following 05.05.1984. The plaintiff Amrita Lal Das never transferred the suit land in favour of the defendant or anybody. The defendant no.'01 filed Other Class Suit No. 53 of 1976 in the Court of the then Munsif, Bajitpur against the plaintiff for specific performance of contract. The defendant no. 01 of that suit filed written statement. The suit was dismissed for default. Thereafter, the plaintiff of that suit filed a Miscellaneous 
Case being No. 49 of 1981 under Order 9 Rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of the suit which was rejected on contest. Subsequently against that order of rejection the plaintiff Samsuddin filed a Miscellaneous Appeal being No. 133 of 1982 which was also dismissed on contest by a judgment and order dated 22.03.1983. Thereafter, the defendants filed Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993. It is the case of the plaintiff that he had no knowledge of Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 which was decreed exparte against him behind his back. Thereafter in a Execution Case being No. 09 of 1981 a sale deed was registered through court on 03.03.1982 A.D. but the decree by virtue of which the sale deed was obtained is the product of fraud and collusion. 
5. The contrary case of the plaintiff-petitioners of Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 is such, that the plaintiff of Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 Amrita Lal Das executed 2(two) separate sale deeds on 27.02.1971 and out of these two deeds one is in respect of 211/2 decimals of land in plot no. 426 in favour of Samsuddin (the defendant no. 01 of Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 and plaintiff no. 02 of Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993) and another. in respect of 13 (thirteen) decimals of land in plot no. 425 and 81/2 decimals of land in favour of the wife of Samsuddin, Rabeya Khatun and Mofiz Uddin, full brother of Samsuddin who is the defendant no. 04 in Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 and the defendant No. 1 in Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 after receiving Tk. 3,000/- (three thousand) against each deed. The possession was delivered in favour of purchasers and it was an understanding among the parties that the executant of the deeds Amrita Lal after obtaining income tax clearance certificate would register the sale deeds but after the execution of the deeds the war of liberation was started and the executant Amrita Lal Das left this country. After liberation of Bangladesh Amrita Lal returned back to Bangladesh but refused to register the 2(two) sale deeds in favour of the vendees i.e. Mofiz Uddin and Rabeya Khatun. Thereafter, the vendees of the deeds Mofizuddin and Rabeya Khatun filed Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 and obtained decree by a competent court of law. In decree execution case the deeds were registered through court. The further case of the petitioners is such that due to illness of Samsuddin he could not appear before the court and in his absence the Other Class Suit No. 53 of 1976 was dismissed for default. By amicable settlement Rabeya Khatun got 21⁄4decimals of land from plot no. 425 and 81⁄4decimals of land from plot no. 426 in all 103/4decimals of land. Mofizuddin got 103⁄4 decimals of land from plot no. 425. Samsuddin got 211⁄2decimals of land and his wife got 103⁄4 decimals of land totalling 323⁄4 decimals of land. After getting the aforesaid portion of land they are residing therein as their dwelling huts. 

6. The present opposite party Amrita Lal Das contested Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 after filing written statement with the same case and contention as in the plaint of Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993. Samsuddin and Rabeya Khatun contested in Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 by filing written statement with their same case and contention as in the plaint of Other Class' Suit No. 69 of 1993. Both the suits were heard analogously and disposed of by a single judgment dated 27.02.1994 by the learned Assistant Judge, Katiadi, Kishoreganj. The trial court dismissed the Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 and decreed the Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993. Being aggrieved, Amrita Lal Das preferred 2(two) Title I Appeals being Nos. 142 of 1994 and 143 of 1994 in the Court of learned District Judge, Kishoreganj which was heard and disposed of by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Kishoreganj. The learned appellate court below after hearing both the two appeals disposed of the same in a single judgment vide the impugned judgment and decree dated 24.11.2001. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree of the learned court of appeal the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners have preferred these two revisional applications under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the Rule. 

8. During hearing of these two revisional applications Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali with Mrs. Rubaiyet Hossain, the learned advocates appeared on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners while Mr. Probir Neogi, the learned advocate appeared on behalf of the defendant-appellant-opposite parties. 

9. The learned advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners submits that the learned appellate court below during disposal of the appeal committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in dismissing Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 of the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Katiadi, Kishoreganj. The learned Additional District Judge, Kishoreganj during disposal of the appeals did not take into consideration of the amendment of plaint in Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 and as such there has been non-consideration of material facts occasioning failure of justice. The learned advocate further submits that the lower appellate court committed gross illegality and irregularity in disposing the appeals and there has been misreading and non-reading of evidence and non-consideration of material facts along with documents on record which has materially affected the decision of the learned lower appellate court occasioning failure of justice. The appellate court below committed an error in dismissing the suit though the opposite party no. 01 did not claim the land decreed in Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioners also submits that the ordering portion of the impugned judgment and decree of the learned lower appellate court is ambiguous and self-contradictory. In the ordering portion of the impugned judgment and decree the learned appellate court below allowed one appeal and disallowed the other appeal which is contradictory with the decree in question. The learned advocate lastly submits that the lower appellate court's findings are upon only one suit i.e. Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 but in fact there are 2(two) suits which are Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 and 68 of 1993. The impugned Judgment & decree was passed on the findings of one suit i.e. 68 of 1993 but the order was given upon both the 2(two) suits. The issues were different in the 2(two) suits but the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Kishoreganj during disposal of the appeals considered only one suit's issues. There is no finding of the appellate court on the suit filed by the petitioners upon confirmation of possession and no issues were discussed even or considered during disposal of the appeals which is a gross illegality and non-consideration of material facts resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Furthermore; the impugned judgment and decree was not given under the purview of Order 41 Rule 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure since the lower appellate court did not deliver his judgment after assessment of evidence on record in its true perspective. The provisions laid down in Section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure also not complied with during disposal of the appeals by the lower appellate court. The observation and findings of the trial court which was given in Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 was not reversed by the lower appellate court after consideration of the evidence on records and without reversing the findings of the trial court in Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 the appellate court below reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court illegally which is perverse in the eye of law and accordingly the impugned judgment and decree is not sustainable in law as well as in facts and the Rules are liable to be made absolute. 

10. As against the aforesaid submissions of the learned counsel for the petitioners the learned advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rules submits that in the ordering portion of the lower appellate court's judgment and decree there has been a bonafide mistake which is an apparent error as well as a clerical mistake. The learned court below disallowed the Other Class Appeal No. 142 of 1994 inadvertently and if we concede and consider as a whole it would be clear that in the order of the lower appellate court is an error on the part of the learned presiding judge. For such mistake the impugned judgment and decree can't be frustrated. Under the purview of Section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure as it is an accidental slip of pen of the learned lower appellate court no separate application is required to rectify the mistake as referred to above. The learned advocate further submits, for mere technicalities no party can suffer for mistake of the court. In this context the learned counsel referred some decisions of our Apex Court reported in 30 DLR (SC) 74 and 43 DLR (AD) 58. The learned counsel for the opposite party lastly submits that in disposal of the appeals the learned lower appellate court committed no illegality or irregularity whatsoever by dint of which it can be held that there has been any misreading or non-reading of evidence or non-consideration of material facts -resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The objection raised from the side of the learned advocate for the petitioners is not tenable for the reason that, if the ordering portion of the appellate court's judgment and decree is read in it's all entirety, it would be clear that it is a typographical mistake/error which can be corrected by this Court under Section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

11. Since the lower appellate court fully considered the oral and documentary evidence. of the parties and after proper sifting of evidence and appreciation of law 1;ecided the merit of the case in favour of the appellants there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree. As the appellate court below is the 'final court of facts and all the material facts on record were thoroughly considered, this court has a little scope to interfere with the findings of the final court of facts which is based on evidence. In this context the learned advocate Mr. Probir Neogi cited several decisions of our Apex Court reported in 2 BLC (AD) 134, 44 DLR (AD) 231, 1996 
BLD (AD) 280. It is settled that findings of fact by the appellate court as the final court of facts on consideration of evidence, whether concurrent or not is immune from interference in revision. The learned advocate for the opposite party further submits that in -Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 the exparte decree of Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 and the sale deed executed by court pursuant to the said exparte decree have been sought to be quashed. When a judgment and decree passed in an earlier suit is assailed in a subsequent separate suit, the scope of the court is determined by Section 44 of the Evidence Act, fraud or collusion and the-findings on fraud 'or collusion are the findings of fact. The learned advocate also submits that so far alleged deed in respect of 211⁄2decimals of land of plot no. 426 in favour of Shamsuddin, no relief is available under law as Other Class Suit No. 53 of 1976 was dismissed. No fresh suit would lie in respect of the said deed. The lower appellate court also considered circumstances of the case. In that view of the matter, no interference is called for as it is the purport of Section 115(1) of C.P.C. that there will be no interference unless failure of justice has occasioned. Findings of trial court as to knowledge of. Amrita Lai regarding Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 has been aptly dealt with by the appellate court and reversed with good reason. It is settled if that an order/decision is otherwise valid, it will not be interfered with in revision simply on the ground that it is non- I speaking and in view of the above facts & circumstances the impugned judgment and decree cannot be interfered with and the Rides are liable to be discharged. 

12. Heard the learned advocates of both sides, perused the case records, exhibited documents, deposition of the witnesses and all other connected papers. 

13. On perusal of the case record it transpires that it is an admitted position that the property originally belonged to Amrita Lal Das and it is the case of the present petitioners that Amrita Lal in the year 1971 executed 2(two) sub-kabala deeds dated 27.02.1971 and it was agreed by the executant Amrita Lal that after getting income tax clearance certificate he would register the instruments in favour of the vendees. But while the war of liberation started the executant of the deeds Amrita Lal left this country for India and after liberation he returned back. After returning back he refused to register the instruments and thereafter the petitioners of these revisional applications instituted an Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 and obtained an exparte decree against the executant of the deed. Subsequently by execution case the deeds were registered through court. The present opposite party denied that he was in the know about the existence of Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 as no summons notice was served upon him and after practicing fraud upon the court behind the back of Amrita Lal the decree was obtained. We have come-across from the documents on record that the Other Class Suit No. 53 o 1976 was dismissed for default on 15.07.1980 and against that dismissal order a miscellaneous case was preferred being no. 49 of 1981 which was also dismissed on 18.02.1982. Against that order of dismissal a miscellaneous appeal being no. 133 of 1982 was filed which was dismissed on 22.03.1983. It further appears from the case records that the opposite party by a sale deed dated 27.02.1971 transferred 13 (thirteen) decimals of land from plot no. 425 and  81⁄2decimals of land from plot no. 426 vide exhibit-`Gha'. The consideration amount of the land measuring 211⁄2decimals was Tk. 3,000/- in favour of the defendant-petitioner nos. 2 and 4 and it is the case of the defendants that after getting the deed registered through court they do possess the same as their dwelling huts. The plaintiff-opposite party in this context denied- the execution of the deeds in favour of the defendant nos. 2 and 4 and it is the case of the plaintiff-opposite party that the deeds are collusive and by practicing fraud upon the court the exparte decree was obtained in respect of the deeds allegedly executed by the owner of the land the plaintiff-opposite party Amrita Lal Das. On perusal of the connected papers it is evident that the Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 was a suit for specific performance of contract and in that suit pursuant to a decree execution case no. 09 of 1981 the deed in respect of 211⁄2decimals of land was finally registered vide exhibit-`kha/2'. In this regard; the present opposite party claims that he did not receive any summons notice in Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 and he was not in the know about the decree execution case no. 09 of 1981. He was also not aware of the registration of deed in favour of the defendants and by practicing fraud on collusion it was obtained by the defendants. In this context, on careful scrutiny over the papers on records it appears that the Other Class Suit being No. 54 of 1976 was filed on 26.02.1976 and in that suit the defendant no. 01 Amrita Lal Das made his appearance on 15.12.1976. An application for time was filed for filing written statement therein and accordingly on 28.03.1977 the written statement was filed by Amritalal Das. The learned trial court in this regard consulted the written statement and other relevant papers and  rightly observed that in the written statement the engaged lower of the defendant Amrita Lal was Mr. Md. Habibul Hoque who after putting his signature therein submitted written statement. It was further observed in the findings of the trial court that the plaintiff to that suit prayed for expert's opinion on the signature of the defendant no. 01 Amrita Lai Das and the application was allowed by the trial court. The trial court vide his order dated 27.09.1977 asked the defendant no. 01 to put his signature in the open court and thereafter Amrita Lal after taking 8(eight) adjournments one by one; was not dare to put his signature before the court of law and finally declined. The learned trial court thereafter legally debarred the defendant no. 01 to put his signature and fixed a date for preliminary hearing of the suit. The defendant remained absent on the date of pre-emptory hearing and accordingly the suit was disposed of on exparte. The trial court after consultation with the case record made a concrete findings in his judgment and decree that despite the plaintiff of Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 claimed that he did not receive any summons notice and behind his back practicing fraud the exparte decree was obtained but on perusal of the connected records it is evident to note that the defendant no. 1 who is the plaintiff of Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 after receiving summons appeared and filed written statement. The very fact was not denied by Amrita Lal in his pleading and it is also not denied that the signature of Amrita Lal as it appears in the written statement of Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 is not of the defendant Amrita Lal Das. Apart from this; in the written statement the engaged lawyer of the plaintiff of Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 put his signature and that the defendant to that suit Samsuddin being plaintiff prior to that filed the Other Class Suit No. 53 of 1976 for specific performance of contract and in that suit the engaged lower of Amrita Lal is Mr. Habibul Hoque. Both the two Other Class Suits being No. 53 of 1976 and 54 of 1976 were filed on the same date and in Other Class Suit No. 53 of 1976 Amrita Lal after his appearance submitted written statement. The circumstantial evidence as it appears from the face of the records goes in favour of the plaintiff of Other Class Suit No. 53 of 1976. The learned trial court in this context considered the factual aspect that between the two suits the defendant of Other Class Suit No. 54 of 1976 was not in the know about the very existence of the suit which is against him is not believable. The learned court below in his findings specifically drawn his emphasis that regarding the alleged fraud and collusion from the side of the executant of the deeds is not supported by the evidence on record rather the conduct and role of the executant of the deeds lead the court to draw an adverse inference against him. 
14. In respect of Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 the observation and findings of the learned trial court is such, that the plaintiff to that suit in his pleading claimed that the defendant nos. 1 and 2 of Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 Shamsuddin and Rabeya Khatun for the first time on 05.05.1984 dispossessed the plaintiff from the disputed property. Be that as it may; the plaintiff to that suit Amrita Lal while submitted his written statement on 15.05.1984 and additional written statement on 13.08.1985 in Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 might have mentioned the alleged fact of dispossession. In respect of possession and dispossession over the disputed property the plaintiff of Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 and the defendant of Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 Amrita Lal Das the same individual furnished two separate statements which are not consistent and identical with his own pleading as of his own case. 

15. In this regard; going through the impugned judgment and decree along with the connected papers including the findings and observation of the trial court as well as lower appellate court the learned advocate for the petitioners during his argument most emphatically has drawn my attention that the learned appellate court apparently without rebutting the findings of the trial court reversed the findings and decision as a whole and reversed the judgment and decree which is perverse in the eye of law and non-consideration of material facts affecting the result of the case. It is noticed from the case record that the issue no. 2 of the Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1993 is practically the main subject matter of the original suits. The pertinent question in consultation with the respective pleading of the parties is such as to whether the original owner of the disputed property Amrita Lal Das actually transferred the suit land in favour of the present defendant-petitioners or not and executed the kabala deeds but subsequently declined to make the deeds registered. The trial court in this context after consulting the evidence led therein from the sides of the respective parties made a clear observation and findings with cogent reasoning’s; which are not rebutted by the appellate court below. The lower appellate court in his findings opined that the petitioners of the present revisional application practiced fraud and collusion in, getting exparte decree in their favour without reversing the observation and findings of the trial court. The very conduct of the appellate court go to show that without applying his judicial mind and without compliance of the mandatory provisions of law as embodied in Order 41 Rule 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure passed the impugned judgment and decree. 
Moreover; on careful scrutiny it is noticed from the case records that the findings of the trial court not even discussed by the lower appellate court in his observation and judgment in deciding the fate of the appeals. The findings and discussions on the material issues of the suits were not rebutted before reversing the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and I have already referred to above that the decisions of the learned Additional District Judge, 314 Court, Kishoreganj is based on mere hypothesis and conjecture without proper discussions of the evidence which were cited in the judgment and findings of the trial court in consultation with the evidence adduced by the parties in support of their respective contentions. 
16. Having regard to the facts, circumstances and discussions referred to above I'm constrained to hold such a view that in disposing the appeals the appellate court below committed gross illegality and irregularity resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Furthermore; the lower appellate court misconstrued the facts of the case specially the documentary evidence as referred to above, while the trial court's findings and decision is based on sufficient tangible, credible evidence. Considering the facts, circumstances and discussions mentioned above I have no way out but to draw such inference that the Rules have got much substance to succeed.
17. In the result; the Rules are made absolute. 

18. The impugned judgment and decree dated 24.11.2001 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Kishoreganj in Other Class Appeal No. 142 of 1994 dismissing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 27.02.1994 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Katiadi, Kishoreganj in Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1993 decreeing the suit and the impugned judgment and decree dated 24.11.2001 passed by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Kishoreganj in Other Class Appeal No.143 of 1994 reversing the judgment and decree dated 27.02.1994 passed by the Assistant Judge, Katiadi, Kishoreganj in Other Class Suit No.68 of 1993 dismissing the suit are hereby set-aside. 

19. The order of stay granted earlier at the time of issuance of the Rule in Civil Revision No.1173 of 2002 stands vacated. 

20. However, there will be no order as to costs. 

21. Communicate the judgment and order at-once to the court concerned for information and necessary action. 

22. Send back the Lower Court's Records immediately.
 
23. This judgment and order will govern both the Civil Revision No.1169 of 2002 and Civil Revision No.1173 of 2002 of this Court. 



End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2495 of 2009
lawyer:
Rokanuddin Mahmud, Senior Advocate (with Shamim Khaled Ahmed, Advocate), instructed by Md. Abu Siddique, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioners 
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate (with Mahbuhey Alam, Senior Advocate), instructed by Chowdhury Md. Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record ----- For Respondent No.1 
For the Respondent Nos. 2-4 ----- Not represented

M/s Bangladesh Catfish Limited and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Sunny fish Agency and Trading and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 9.6.2008 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 95 of 2006)
full_judgment:
S.K. Sinha J:- The delay in filing this leave petition is condoned. This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 9th June, 2008 of a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 95 of 2006 affirming with modification of those dated 16th November, 2005 of the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in Money Suit No. 16 of 2004.

2. Respondent No. 1 Sunny 'Fish Agency and Trading (plaintiff) instituted the suit for recovery of Tk. 6,18,57,952 with interest pendent elite against the petitioners (defendants) and the respondent No. 2 (defendant No. 1). Its case in short is that the defendant No. 7 appointed the plaintiff as its sole agent to supply fish feed produced.by it to different fish producing firms by a deed of agreement executed on 31st January, 2005. Plaintiff supplied fish feed to defendant Nos. 2-4 during the period between 2000 and 2001, but the defendants did not pay the price despite repeated demands. Defendant No.1 assured the plaintiff to resolve the matter and requested it to continue the supply of fish feed but the defendant No.1 did not make any arrangement for payment of outstanding price. Ultimately the defendent No. 2 , owed a sum of Tk. 1,87,50,165/- till 21st December, 2002; the defendant No. 3 owed Tk. 3,0056,419/-.till December, 2002 and the defendant No. 4 owed Tk. 80,51,428/- , which they refused to pay. 

3. Defendants contested the suit by filing separate written statements. Case of the defendant No. 1 is that it never issued any letter of comfort to the plaintiff to pay the dues against the supply of fish feed to the defendant Nos. 2-4 and there-fore it is not under any obligation to pay money to the plaintiff. The other defendant Nos. 2-4 in their written statements have admitted that the defendant No. 7 is a fish feed producing organisation and the plaintiff has been acting as its agent on commission basis and that the plaintiff has supplied fish feed to them on different occasions. Their case is that the plaintiff used to collect the price of the fish feed from time to time but as the plaintiff was liable to pay to the defendant No. 7 an amount of Tk. 5,54,69,729/- against the price of the fish feed supplied by the defendant No. 7 they are not liable to pay the outstanding price to the plaintiff as claimed other than the commission that it was legally entitled to from the defendant No. 7. Defendant No. 3 took a different plea in its written statement. It is stated that while the plaintiff was supplying the fish feed the affairs of it's company was being managed by the defendant No. 7 and assumed it's liability by executing an agreement. The defendant No. 3 having incurred huge loss, it became a losing concern and the plaintiff knowing the said financial condition supplied the fish feed at its risk, and that the defendant No. 1 could not avoid the liability since it assumed the entire liability. 

4. On consideration of the materials on record the learned Joint District Judge by judgment and order dated 16th November,2005 decreed Tk. 2,47,50, 109.60 against the defendant No. 2, Tk. 4,62,74,473 against the defendant No. 3 and Tk. 1,6,27,884 .96 against the defendant No. 4 totaling Tk. 8,60,52, 496.56 holding that the defendant Nos. 1,2,3 and 4 are jointly liable to pay 11.7 the said amount to the plaintiff with interest. 

5. Defendant No. 1 Saudi Bangladesh Industrial and Agricultural Investment Co. Ltd. preferred First Appeal No. 53 of 2006, the defendant Nos. 2-4 preferred First Appeal No. 95 of 2006, and the defendant No. 7 .preferred First Appeal No. 97 of 2006 against the judgment and decree of the High Court Division. The High Court Division heard all the appeals analogously and disposed of them by judgment and order dated 9th June, 2008. The High Court Division allowed First Appeal No. 53 of 2006 in part and dismissed First Appeal No. 95 of 2006 with modification and set aside the judgment and decree of the Joint District Judge so far as it relates to passing decree against the defendant No. 1 as well, but reduced the amounts of the decree to Tk. 1,87,50,105/- in place of 2,47,50,138.60 passed against the defendant No. 2, Tk. 3,50,56,419/- in place of 4,62,74,473/- against the defendant No. 3 and Tk. 80,51,428/- in place of Tk. 1,6,27,884.96 against the defendant No. 4, totaling Tk. 6,18,57,952/- in place of Tk. 8,16,52,496.56/. 

6. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioners contended that the learned Judges of the High Court Division erred in law in affirming the judgment and decree with modification passed by the learned Joint District Judge in failing to notice that the affairs of the defendant Nos. 2-4 having been taken over by the defendant No. 1, the defendant-petitioners are not under any obligation to pay the price of the fish feed to the plaintiff, if there be any, and therefore, the decree has rendered infructuous. Learned Counsel further contended that admittedly the plaintiff had acted as an agent of the defendant No. 7 and supplied the fish feed to the petitioners on commission basis and since the plaintiff owed Tk. 5 crore an odd to the defendant No. 7, the learned Judges of the High Court Division ought to have modified the decree to the extent the plaintiff was legally entitled to com-mission of 9% out of the total decrial amount. 

7. We would like to observe here that the plaintiff did not take any exception against the judgment of the High Court Division so far as it relates to exonerating the defendant No. 1 from the payment of the decreetal amount jointly with the defendant Nos. 2-4 and also of the modification of the amounts decreed by the learned Joint District Judge. The defendants did riot dispute the plaintiffs claim that it supplied the fish feed on taking credit from defendant No. 7 and also non payment of the price of fish feed to the plaintiff. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, in the premises, on consideration of this admitted fact held as under: "From the impugned judgment it appears that defendant Nos. 2-4 failed to show that they did not take the fish feed from the plaintiff and thus they were not liable to pay the dues as claimed by the plaintiff. Rather in the respective written statements filed by them they have clearly admitted the fact of their receipt of the fish feed from the plaintiff. These defendants never took the plea that they paid back the money due to plaintiff against such supply of fish feed to them. Mr. Shamim Khaled also failed to show by referring to the evidence on record that the finding of the learned Joint District Judge as to the liabilities of defendant Nos. 2-4 to pay the dues to the plaintiffs to the tune of Tk. 1,87,50,105, Tk. 3,50,56,1419 and Tk. 80,51,428 respectively was wrong either being based on non consideration of any material evidence or on misreading or misconstruction of any such evidence. On consideration of the evidence on record adduced by the plaintiff it appears to us that the findings of the learned Joint District Judge in that respect are based on proper reading of the evidence on record which are all documentary and we have nothing to interfere with the said finding. In this regard it is necessary to keep on record that the plea taken. by defendant Nos. 2-4 in their respective written statements was that as the plaintiff owed money to defendants against the taking of fish feed from it on credit so it was not entitled to get any money from them (defendant Nos. 2-4). We are of the view that since defendant Nos. 2-4 took fish feed from the plaintiff it was their obligation to pay the dues to the plaintiff and they in no way could escape their liability on the ground of nonpayment of the dues of defendant No. 7 and that has nothing to do with the dues of defendant Nos. 2-4." 

8. As regards the submission of Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud that since the plaintiff was liable to pay Tk. 5,54,69,743/- to the defendant No. 7 which supplied the fish feed on credit to the plaintiff, the defendant are not liable to pay to the plaintiff is devoid of sub-stance, inasmuch as, this is not an issue in this suit, and as the plaintiff did not make any claim against the defendant No. 1, there is no scope on the part of the defendant No. 7 to make counter claim against the plaintiff. In this regard the trial court observed that an arbitration proceeding is pending between the plaintiff and defendant No. 7. On the other hand, the learned Judges of the High Court Division observed that the plaintiff having not claimed any relief against the defendant No. 7, any finding relating to the transaction between the plaintiff and defendant No. 7 is uncalled for. We fully agree with the views taken by the learned Judges of the High Court Division. If the plaintiff owed any amount to the defendant No. 7 towards the price of fish feed supplied on credit that will not disentitle the plaintiff to get a decree against the defendants who admittedly received fish feed from the plaintiff but did not repay the price. 

9. The defendant-petitioners did not deny their liability towards the price of fish feed being supplied by the plaintiff. The defendants failed to produce any documentary evidence to show that there was any tripartite agreement amongst the plaintiff on the one part, the defendant Nos. 2-4 on the 2nd part and the defendant No. 7 on the 3rd part pro-viding that the plaintiff would supply fish feed to the defendant Nos. 2-4 taking on credit from the defendant No. 7 on the condition that the plaintiff would be entitled to 9% commission only out of the price of the fish feed and that the defendant Nos. 2-4 would pay to the defendant No. 7 the total price of the fish feed supplied by the plaintiff excluding the commission, that could have been a ground to avoid the payment of the Dec rectal amount directly to the plaintiff. The transaction was between the plaintiff and defendants and the latter had acquiescence to the receipt of fish feed on credit from the plaintiff and therefore, they can not avoid the liability of payment of the price of fish feed to the plaintiff. If there be any dispute between the plaintiff and the defendant No. 7 over the payment of price of the fish feed, it would be decided in a properly constituted suit between them but, that will not be a ground for the defendants to withhold the payment of the decreetal amount. We find no merit in the contention of Mr. Mahmud. 

10. The petition is accordingly dismissed. 

End.
